Paulastya, Apratima, Nābhāga Kāśyapa, Āṅgirasa, Nabhas, and Satya—these seven are the supreme ṛṣis. || 56 ||
There were two hosts of deities, as well as those who are remembered as the seers and the mantras:
Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, the heroic Bhūriṣeṇa,
Śatānīka, Nīrāmitra, Vṛṣasena, and Jayadratha.
Bhūridyumna and Suvarcas— these ten were the sons of Manu.
In the eleventh period,
however, [there were] eleven.
In the interval of the third [kalpa], there were Manus. (58)
Indeed, during the third Sāvarṇa [Manvantara]. || 58 ||
The Nirmāṇarati gods are indeed born of desire and possess the speed of thought;
these are known as the three groups of high-souled deities. || 58 ||
Each of those groups of thirty inhabitants of the triple heaven corresponds to the thirty days that the wise know to be in a month. || 582 ||
The gods will be the Nirmāṇaratis, and the birds will be the nights. This shall be the third group of deities that will come into being. || 583 ||
The moments (muhūrta) are indeed called "swift as thought" (manojava); these are proclaimed as the gods.
For they are remembered as the future Manus, the sons of Brahmā. || 584 ||
From them, Indra shall be born as the future king of the gods, named Vṛṣa.
Learn now of his seven sages as they are being proclaimed:
Haviṣmān Kāśyapa, and Vapuṣmān Bhārgava; || 59 ||
Vāruṇi, as well as Ātreya, Vāsiṣṭha, and Anagha;
Puṣṭi is to be known as belonging to Aṅgiras, and likewise Niścara belongs to Paulastya. || 60 ||
Paulaha and Agnitejas—these Paulaha and Agnitejas are to be the seven great seers (maharṣis) during the eleventh interval of the gods. || 61 ||
The gods are the sons of Brahmā; three groups of them are recorded. || 61 ||
Sarvātraga, Suśarman, Devānīka, Purovaha, Kṣemadhanvan, Dṛḍhāyu, Ādarśa, Pauṇḍraka, and Manu. (62)
Nine sons are indeed recorded for the third Sāvarṇi; now,
for the fourth Sāvarṇi...
Learn from me concerning the seven sages: || 63 ||
Now, those nine sons of Sāvarṇa, the son of Prajāpati,
[shall arise] in the twelfth period.
Of Manu, the son of Rudra. || 63 ||
The fourth is Rudrasāvarṇi; hear now of the gods during his interval:
five groups of deities are said to belong to the future. || 631 ||
The Haritas, the Rohitas, the Devas, the Sumanasas, and the Sukarmans and Sutāras—these are remembered as the five classes of gods. || 632 ||
For these are the mind-born sons of Brahmā, each consisting of a group of ten:
Aruṃtuda, Havis, Vidvān, and Sahasradā.
Parvata, Anucara, Apāṃśu, Manojava, Ūrjā, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Tārā—these ten are known as the Haritas. || 634 ||
Tapas, Jñānin, Mṛti, Varcas, and Bandhu are those who are remembered; likewise Rajas, Rāja, and Svarṇapāda. (635)
Vyuṣṭi and Vidhi—these ten gods are remembered as the Rohitas;
those gods beginning with the Tuṣitas who are proclaimed to be thirty-three in number, || 636 ||
One should know the gods to be well-disposed. Listen, O you of good deeds: Suparvan, Vṛṣabha, Pṛṣṭa, Kapidyumna, and Vipaścit. || 637 ||
Vikrama, Krama, Vibhūta, and Kānta—these are gods of virtuous deeds. Now learn of the Sutāras: || 638 ||
Varṣa, Divya, Añjiṣṭha, Varcasvin, Dyutimat, Kavi, Śubha, Havis, Kṛtaprāpti, and Vyāpuṭa as the tenth. || 639 ||
These gods are indeed proclaimed by name as the Sutārās;
their Indra should be known as the highly illustrious Ṛtadhāman. || 6310 ||
Dyuti was the son of Vasiṣṭha, while Sutapas was likewise of Atri's lineage;
Tapomūrti was of Aṅgiras's line, and Tapasvin was of Kaśyapa's.
The son of Pulastya was Tapodhana, the son of Pulaha was Taporati, and the seventh among them, the descendant of Bhṛgu, should be known as Tapodhṛti. || 65 ||

Five groups of gods are proclaimed; these are the seven ṛṣis, the Siddhas, the mind-born sons of Brahmā. In the final Sāvarṇika interval, [the sons will be] Devavān, Upadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and Vidūratha. (66)
Mitravān, Mitravindu, Mitrāsena, Amitrahā, Mitrabāhu, and Suvarcas were the sons of Manu, the twelfth [Manu]. || 67 ||
But in the thirteenth cycle, during the period of Raucya, it shall be manifested once again.
Only three classes of gods were proclaimed by the Self-Existent One;
for all those high-souled ones were the mind-born sons of Brahmā. || 68 ||
Those three—the Sutrāmaṇas, the Sudharmas, and the Sukarmas—are declared to be the future hosts of the thirty gods who drink the soma juice. || 68 ||
The thirty-three deities who are worshipped separately by the ritualists—with clarified butter, speckled butter, and indeed with the most excellent cup (graha)—[are all present here]. || 68 ||
As for those gods who are thirty-three, understand them according to their distinct categories:
the Sutramanas, the Prayājyas, and those who are currently the Ājyapas. || 68 ||

Those who perform good deeds are the Anuyājyas; those who consume the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) are the Upayājyas; and those of virtuous conduct are the Sudharmas—thus are the gods proclaimed. || 68 ||
Divaspati, the Great Being, will be their Indra.
Those sons of the son of Pulaha are to be known as the offspring of Ruci.
Aṅgiras, the steadfast Dhṛtimat, the imperishable Paulastya, the truth-seeing Paulaha, and the dispassionate Bhārgava. (69)
Niṣprakampa, likewise Atreya, Nirmoha, Kāśyapa, and Sutapas Vāsiṣṭha—these seven are indeed the great ṛṣis. || 70 ||
The Self-existent One has declared that there are exactly three classes of deities.
These sons of Ruci are to be known as the offspring of the thirteenth [Manu].
Citrasena, Vicitra, Naya, Dharmabhṛt, Dhṛta, Sunetra, Kṣatravṛddhi, Sutapas, Nirbhaya, and Dṛḍha. || 71 ||
These were the sons of Raucya Manu during the thirteenth interval;
and in the fourteenth cycle, during the interval of Manu Bhautya himself—72.
The five groups of deities that will come into being have been declared:
the Cākṣuṣas, the Pavitras, the Kaniṣṭhas, and likewise the Bhrājiras.
And those who are advanced in speech—these are remembered as the five classes of gods.
The seven notes, beginning with *niṣāda*, are the seven *vidhis* belonging to the *Cākṣuṣa* [Manvantara]. || 72 ||
They know those seven youngest ones as the Sāmans beginning with the Bṛhat;
they are the seven pure worlds, the radiant seven rivers. || 72 ||
Know that the sages who are advanced in speech belong indeed to Svāyambhuva Manu;
all the Indras of the various Manvantaras are to be understood as possessing identical characteristics.
In splendor, ascetic power, intellect, strength, learning, and valor—whatever beings there are in the three worlds, whether moving or stationary—[are surpassed by him]. || 72 ||

By their own qualities, those Indras indeed surpass all others. Among the disputants, the three Vedas are the foremost: those who delight in censuring existing things, those who remain indifferent while speaking of existing things, and those who are devoted to repeating what already exists. || 72 ||
Agnīdhra was Kāśyapa, as was Paulastya Māgadha;
Agnibāhu was Bhārgava, and likewise Śuci was Āṅgirasa. (73)
And likewise here are Yukta, Atri, Śukra, Vasiṣṭha, Ajita, Paulaha, and those who are the final seven ṛṣis. || 74 ||
By reciting these at dawn, one's happiness increases;
one attains great renown and likewise becomes long-lived. || 75 ||
O bull of the Bharatas, it is said that for the great sages of the past and the future, as well as for the hosts of deities, there are always five classes of men.
Tarāṅgabhīru, Bradhna, Tarasmanugra, Abhimānin, Pravīṇa, Jīṣṇu, and likewise Saṃkrandana. || 77 ||
Tejasvin and Sabala—these are the sons of Bhautya Manu. Indeed, these four Sāvarṇa Manus are the sons of Brahmā.
Vaivasvata alone is called Sāvarṇa Manu;
and those two, Raucya and Bhautya, are considered to be the sons of Pulaha and Bhṛgu respectively.
When the period of Bhautya’s authority is completed, the Kalpa is fulfilled. || 78 ||
Thus have these Manus of the future and the past been proclaimed by me;
by them this entire earth, extending to the edge of the ocean and including its cities, [was governed].
O best of the twice-born, having protected [the world] for a full thousand yugas by means of his subjects and his own austerity, he constantly effects their dissolution. || 80 ||
Those seventy-one yugas, including the Kṛta, Tretā, and others, are said to constitute the interval of a Manu. (81)
These fourteen Manus have been celebrated as increasers of fame;
they are all sovereign lords throughout the Vedas and the Purāṇas. (82)
The lords of creatures are the wise ones; their glorification brings merit.
During the Manvantaras there are destructions, and at the end of those destructions there are regenerations.
O twice-born ones, it is indeed impossible to state the end of the emission and the reabsorption of living beings, even in hundreds of years.
O best of the twice-born, it is heard that at the end of each Manvantara there are destructions;
therein the gods remain along with the seven sages, leaving a remnant behind.
Endowed with austerity, celibacy, and sacred learning, when a thousand yugas are complete, the kalpa is said to be entirely exhausted. || 86 ||
There, O twice-born ones, all beings were scorched by the rays of the sun; placing Brahmā at their head, they departed together with the hosts of Ādityas.
They enter again and again at the ends of the kalpas into Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, the foremost of gods and the creator of all beings. 88.
The unmanifest is the eternal God; this entire world belongs to him.
In this regard, I shall proclaim to you the lineage of Manu Vaivasvata. 89.
O tigers among the lords of sages, I shall now relate the ancient account of the present one of great splendor, as it occurs in connection with this lineage. || 90 ||
Therein was born that high-souled Hari, the Lord of the Vṛṣṇi clan, for the destruction of all asuras and for the welfare of all the worlds. || 91 ||
## Section 4. The Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 1 The highly illustrious Vivasvat was born from Kaśyapa by Dākṣāyaṇī.
Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter, the goddess Saṃjñā, became the wife of that Vivasvat. || 1 ||
She was renowned as Sureśvarī; that illustrious lady was known as Sureṇu throughout the three worlds. She was again celebrated by the name Saṃjñā;
she indeed became the wife of the high-souled Lord Mārtaṇḍa. || 2 ||

Though endowed with beauty and youth, Saṃjñā was not satisfied with the form of her husband; for that form of the Sun, possessed of intense splendor, was like the blazing orb of the sun itself. || 3 ||
"Though his limbs were completely scorched, he did not appear as if he had passed away;
out of affection, she said, 'Surely this one is not dead while still in the egg.'"
Because Kaśyapa did not know [this], he is therefore called Mārtaṇḍa;
moreover, the splendor of that Vivasvat is eternally exceeding. || 5 ||
By whom, the son of Kaśyapa, the best among those who radiate heat, scorched the three worlds; O Brahmin, that Ravi begot three offspring upon Saṃjñā— yes,
three offspring upon Saṃjñā.
Āditya begot two sons of great prowess and two Prajāpatis, as well as a daughter, Kalindī;
and first [he begot] Manu Vaivasvata, the Prajāpati Śrāddhadeva.
Yama and Yamunā were born; from them, Yama and Yamī were born as twins. Seeing that dark-complexioned form of Vivasvat’s, Saṃjñā [was distressed].
But being unable to endure her own shadow, she then created another woman of the same appearance;
that woman was composed of illusion, while that other woman was made of the earth, from whom the shadow had arisen. (9) From her, the shadow emerged. (9)
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence,
Chāyā spoke to Saṃjñā: "O best of the twice-born,
what must be done by me?"
Speak, O lady of pure smiles!
I stand at your command; instruct me, O woman of excellent complexion! (10)
Saṃjñā said: "I shall go, may you be blessed, to my father's own abode;
you must dwell in my place in the house with an unchanging mind. || 11 ||
"These two boys of mine and this slender-waisted girl shall be entrusted to you; you must not speak of this to the Blessed One. || 12 ||
Savarṇā said:
"O Goddess, until my hair is seized, or until a curse is pronounced, I shall never disclose your secret intention; go, O Goddess, as you please! (13)
Having thus instructed Savarṇā, and having been told "So be it" by her,
that ascetic woman went into the presence of Tvaṣṭṛ as if filled with shame.
But she, having gone into her father's presence, was then rebuked by her father;
she was repeatedly urged, "Go to your husband's side. || 15 ||
Then that blameless woman, having assumed the form of a mare and concealed her true appearance, went to the Northern Kurus and began to graze upon the grass. || 16 ||
While reflecting upon the second designation, thinking "this is the name," the Sun then begot a son equal to himself. || 17 ||
O Brahmins, because this lord was considered equal to his predecessor Manu,
he became Manu by name and is called Sāvarṇi. || 18 ||
The second son born of her is to be known as Śanaiścara; she,
indeed, was the earthly Saṃjñā.
Then, indeed, [he spoke] to his own son. || 19 ||
Manu indeed felt greater affection for her than for his elder sons;
however, Yama could not tolerate that. || 20 ||
Out of anger, out of childishness, and by the force of destiny yet to come, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, threatened Saṃjñā with his foot.
Then, out of anger, Sāvarṇi’s mother, being deeply distressed, cursed him: "Wandering about, you shall fall upon a stone slab! (22)
Śrutaśravas will be their son;
he will indeed be Sāvarṇi. || 18 ||
Śrutakarmā is to be known as the planet Śanaiścara;
Saṃjñā, however, is their earthly [consort].
Just as he acted toward his own sons, || 19 ||
She did not show affection for those born before her; yet,
because you threaten them with your foot, she has acted thus.
[He struck] the illustrious wife of his father;
therefore, this foot of yours will fall [upon you], there is no doubt. || 22 ||
Yama, however, with palms joined in reverence, reported all of that to his father;
Yama, moreover, by that curse—
With his mind deeply afflicted,
the righteous-souled one reported everything concerning his father to Manu.
Greatly agitated by the fear of the curse, he was dissuaded by the words of Saṃjñā.
"May this curse be averted," he then said to his father; [the father replied], "Out of affection for their mother, [all beings] act toward everyone..."
One should indeed behave [in this manner] toward one's sons. || 24 ||
O King, our mother does not behave toward us with equal affection. || 24 ||
She, having abandoned us, desires to become the junior wife. My foot was raised against her, but it was not brought down upon her body. || 25 ||
Whether out of childishness or through delusion, you ought to forgive that!
O Lord of the World, best among those who radiate heat, I have been cursed by my mother;
by your grace, O Lord of Cows, may my foot not fall [to the ground]! (26)
Vivasvat said:
"Without doubt, my son, there must be a great cause for this, by which anger has taken possession of you, who are a knower of dharma and a speaker of truth. || 27 ||
It is not possible to make these words of your mother false;
however, worms shall take the flesh and depart into the earth. || 28 ||
Then, O highly wise one, you shall again obtain your feet in comfort;
thus your mother’s word shall indeed be made true. || 29 ||
"And by the removal of the curse, you shall also be saved.
Āditya then said to Saṃjñā: "Why indeed [have you acted thus] toward your children? (30)
"Why do you show such excessive affection for one among those who are equal?
She, however, avoiding that [question], did not speak of Vivasvat. || 31 ||
Having composed his self through yoga, he beheld the truth;
the Lord, the Master, desiring to curse her and enraged for her destruction, [looked upon her]. (32)
And she seized him by his hair; then, when the appointed time had passed, she related everything to Vivasvat exactly as it had occurred.
Then Vivasvat, having heard that, went in anger to Tvaṣṭṛ. || 33 ||
But Tvaṣṭṛ, having honored that Vibhāvasu according to the prescribed rites, then indeed pacified him who was desirous of burning everything down in his wrath. || 34 ||
Tvaṣṭṛ said:
"This form of yours, pervaded by excessive brilliance, is not beautiful; unable to endure it, Saṃjñā wanders in the grassy forest. (35)
"O Lord of the Cowherds, by resorting to yoga, you shall today behold your own wife, who is of auspicious conduct, praiseworthy, and endowed with the power of yoga."
But it is not agreeable to you, O Lord;
if it were so, then according to my opinion, O subduer of enemies, I shall today transform your lovely form. || 37 ||
Then, by agreement, Tvaṣṭṛ placed Vivasvat Mārtaṇḍa upon a lathe and indeed whetted away his brilliance. || 38 ||
Then that form, manifested by the concentrated splendor, shone even more brilliantly as it was beheld, becoming more lovely than the most lovely. || 39 ||
Applying himself to yoga, he beheld his own wife in the form of a mare,
unassailable by all beings due to her splendor and her self-restraint.

O Brahmins, as she wandered about free from fear in the form of a mare, Mārtaṇḍa, assuming the form of a horse, united with her at the mouth; for she was making advances for sexual union, suspecting him to be another man. || 41 ||
She discharged that unsurpassed semen from her nostrils for Vivasvat;
from it were born the two gods, the Aśvins, the best among physicians. || 42 ||
Nāsatya and Dasra are remembered as the two Aśvins;
they are the two sons of Mārtaṇḍa, the eighth Prajāpati. || 43 ||
The Sun-god revealed himself to her in his lovely form;
and upon seeing her husband, she was both delighted and overcome with infatuation. || 44 ||
But Yama, his mind deeply distressed by that curse, gratified these subjects through righteousness, O Dharmarāja. || 45 ||
By that auspicious deed, he of supreme splendor obtained sovereignty over the ancestors as well as the status of a world-protector.
Manu Sāvarṇi was indeed that Prajāpati of great renown;
he is to become the Manu in the future Sāvarṇika interval.
The sage discharged it from his mouth, but he deposited that semen in his nostrils.
Even today, the Lord performs severe penance on the summit of Mount Meru.
His brother Śanaiścara attained the status of a planet. || 48 ||
Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned Viṣṇu’s discus with that splendor, so that it might be irresistible in battle through his desire for the destruction of the Dānavas. || 49 ||
The younger of the two, the illustrious maiden Yamī, became the Yamunā, the best of rivers, who purifies the world. || 50 ||
He who is called Manu in the world, the eldest and most radiant, is also known as Śāvarṇa; his creation is the present one. I shall describe in detail that which is the second son of him [Manu].
Śanaiścara was the brother of Manu, the son of Vivasvat. || 52 ||
He indeed attained the status of a planet, being honored by all the worlds. || 50 ||
Whoever should hear or recite this account of the birth of the gods shall be liberated from calamity upon encountering it and shall attain great renown. || 51 ||
## Section 4: Vaṃśānucarita | Chapter 2 | Part A The sons of Vaivasvata Manu were indeed nine, equal to him:
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Śaryāti; || 1 ||
Narīṣyanta, Prāṃśu, Nābhāga, Ariṣṭa as the seventh, Karūṣa, and Pṛṣadhra—these nine are remembered as the Mānavas. || 2 ||
O Brahmins, the high-minded Manu, the Lord of Creatures, desiring sons, performed a sacrifice for Mitra and Varuṇa even before this.
O twice-born ones, while these nine sons had not yet been born,
and while that sacrifice was still in progress, O best of the twice-born.
In the portion belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa, Manu offered an oblation;
there appeared a woman wearing celestial garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
And Ilā was born with a divine constitution; such is the sacred tradition. Then Manu Daṇḍabhara addressed her as "Ilā": || 6 ||
"Follow me, O blessed lady! Ilā replied to that Prajāpati who desired a son, with these words endowed with righteousness: || 7 ||
She said: "O best of speakers, I was born from a portion of Mitra and Varuṇa;
I shall go into their presence, lest Dharma, being violated, destroy us. (8)
Having spoken thus to the god Manu,
Ilā, the beautiful woman, approached Mitrā-Varuṇa and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words: || 9 ||
"O gods, I am born as a portion of you both; what may I do for you? I have been told by Manu himself: 'Follow after me! (10)
To that virtuous Ilā, who spoke thus and was devoted to dharma,
both Mitra and Varuṇa [replied].
The two best of the twice-born said to her: || 11 ||
"O knower of dharma, O lady of beautiful form, we are both pleased by this humility, self-restraint, and truthfulness of yours. || 12 ||
O highly fortunate lady, you shall attain renown as "Vayō," a maiden;
moreover, you alone shall become the son who perpetuates the lineage of Manu.
Renowned as Sudyumna, he was honored throughout the three worlds; beloved by the world, virtuous in character, he increased the lineage of Manu. || 14 ||
Having heard that, she turned back. But that goddess, having obtained the boon, while going toward her father’s presence, turned back toward her father;
then Budha, finding an opportunity, invited her for sexual union. || 15 ||

From Budha, the son of Soma, Aila Purūravas was born upon her. Having given birth to him from Budha, she (Ilā) then attained the state of being Sudyumna. She attained the state of being Sudyumna once again. || 16 ||
Sudyumna had three heirs who were supremely righteous:
Utkala, Gaya, and likewise Vinatāśva. || 17 ||
The kingdom of Utkala belongs to Utkala, and the western quarter belongs to Vinatāśva;
the eastern direction belongs to that royal sage, while the city of Gayā belongs to Gaya. || 18 ||
But once Manu had entered [the ark] and created the subjects, he assigned that solar power tenfold and made this earth his domain. || 19 ||
Ikṣvāku, the eldest heir, obtained the Middle Country;
however, Sudyumna, because he was female, did not obtain any portion at all. || 20 ||
But by the word of Vasiṣṭha, the highly effulgent and great-souled Sudyumna established his capital at Pratiṣṭhāna as the sovereign of righteousness. || 21 ||
Having obtained that kingdom, the highly illustrious son of Manu, who was possessed of great fortune and endowed with the auspicious marks of both male and female, bestowed it upon Purūravas.
"He who held [the earth] was known as Ila and likewise as Sudyumna.
Having heard this, the sages then questioned him further.
But how did that Sudyumna, a man, come to attain the state of a woman? || 22 ||
Sūta said: In ancient times, Sanaka and the other Kumāras went to Ilāvṛta to see Maheśvara, and there they beheld the one whose banner is the bull.
Seeing him sporting with Umā in that secluded place, everyone then departed; and Śivā also became ashamed. || 22 ||
For the sake of her beloved, the dear goddess spoke these words:
"O Lord, whatever man shall enter this hermitage of mine," || 224 ||
She will certainly become a woman, auspicious and equal to the Apsarases;
there, all beings—whether Piśācas or animals—[will be present]. || 225 ||
Having become women, they sported with Rudra like celestial nymphs (apsarases).
But that king, having gone out on a hunt, entered Umā’s grove. || 226 ||
When Rudra had assumed the form of a woman along with the *piśācas* and *bhūtas*, King Sudyumna consequently attained the female state once more;
yet, through the grace of Mahādeva, he regained his status as a man. || 227 ||
The Śakas were the sons of Nariṣyanta, O twice-born ones; but the sons of Nābhāga were the Bhojas. || 23 ||
Ambarīṣa was born as his son,
the most excellent among the bulls of kings;
from Dhṛṣṭa came the Dhārṣṭaka kṣatriyas.
He indeed became bold in battle. || 24 ||
Learn in detail the natural disposition of the sons of Manu!
Pṛṣadhra, however, having killed his guru’s cow, ate its flesh at night.
Having fallen to the status of a Śūdra due to the curse of the high-souled Cyavana, the Kārūṣas became Kṣatriyas under Karūṣa, fierce in battle. || 24 ||
A host of a thousand kṣatriyas was born, full of prowess.
Nābhāga’s son was the learned Udaṅka, who had Bhalandana as his son. || 24 ||
Bhalandana had a son named Prāṃśu, who was possessed of great strength;
Prāṃśu had an only son, renowned as Prajāni. || 244 ||
Prajāni had a son named Khanitra, who was full of valor;
his son was the illustrious and highly renowned Kṣupa. || 245 ||
Viṃśa was indeed the son of Kṣupa, and he became Pratimāna;
Viṃśa’s son was the virtuous Kalyāṇa, named Viviṃśa. || 246 ||
The son of Viviṃśa was the righteous and powerful Khaninetra;
his son was Kharandhama, who appeared at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga. || 247 ||
And the sons of Kharandhama were also known as the Āvikṣitas; among them was the powerful Āvikṣita, who surpassed his father in virtue. || 248 ||
The righteous king named Marutta, who was equal to a universal monarch, was led to heaven by Saṃvarta along with his friends and kinsmen. || 249 ||
A great dispute arose here between Saṃvarta and Bṛhaspati;
having seen the prosperity of that sacrifice, Bṛhaspati became enraged. || 2410 ||
When the sacrifice was seized by Saṃvarta, he then became exceedingly enraged;
for he [was intent] upon the destruction of the worlds, though he was indeed pacified by the deities. || 2411 ||
Marutta was a universal monarch; he obtained Narīṣyanta as his son.
The heir of Narīṣyanta was King Daṇḍadhāra Damaka. || 2412 ||
His son was the valiant King Rāṣṭravardhana;
his son was Sudhṛti, and from Sudhṛti came Nara. || 2413 ||
Kevala was his son, and Bandhumān was the son of Kevala;
then the son of Bandhumān was the righteous king Vegavān. || 2414 ||
Budha was the son of Vegavat, and Tṛṇabindu was the son of Budha;
he became king at the beginning of the third age, the Tretā Yuga. || 2415 ||
Kaṇyā was his mother, for she was the daughter of Viśravas;
and his sons were born of her, among whom Viśāla became a most righteous king.
The bountiful King Hemacandra, of renowned heroism and vigor, the mighty son of Viśāla, by whom Viśālā was founded. || 2417 ||
Sucandra, renowned as such, followed immediately after Hemacandra;
Sucandra’s son was the king celebrated as Dhūmrāśva. || 2418 ||
The learned Śṛñjaya was born as the son of Dhūmrāśva;
the illustrious and powerful Sahadeva was the son of Śṛñjaya. || 2419 ||
Kṛśāśva was the son of Sahadeva and was supremely righteous;
Kṛśāśva’s son was the highly energetic and powerful Somadatta.
The son of the royal seer Somadatta was Janamejaya;
and the son of Janamejaya was the renowned Pramāti by name. || 2421 ||
By the grace of Tṛṇabindu, all the kings of Vaiśālī were indeed long-lived, high-souled, heroic, and very righteous. || 2422 ||
Śaryāti had a pair of children: a son renowned by the name Ānarta, and a daughter named Sukanyā, who became the wife of Cyavana. || 25 ||
The heir of Ānarta was the highly effulgent one named Reva;
he possessed the territory of Ānarta, and his capital city was Kuśasthalī. || 26 ||
Reva’s son was the righteous Raivata, named Kakudmin;
he was the eldest of a hundred sons, and having obtained the kingdom, he ruled from Kuśasthalī. || 27 ||
Accompanied by his daughter, he heard from Brahmā that what had been but a moment for the Lord was many yugas for a mortal. || 28 ||
Then, while still a youth, he returned to his own city, which was surrounded by the Yādavas, named Dvāravatī, possessing many gates and enchanting to the mind. (29)

[The city] was protected by the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, with Vāsudeva at their head. Then, O best of the twice-born, having heard that report exactly as it had happened, Raivata, the subduer of enemies, understood the truth of the matter.
Having given that maiden named Revatī, who was firm in her vows, to Baladeva,
he went to the peak of Mount Meru and established himself in ascetic practice.
The righteous Rāma also lived happily, accompanied by Revatī.
The sages said: Having heard that story, the sages then asked: || 32 ||
O Mahāmati, how is it that after many eons have passed, old age did not overtake Revatī nor the humped Raivata? || 33 ||
How did the lineage of that Śaryāti, who had gone to Mount Meru, remain on earth even until today? We wish to hear this according to the truth! (34)
Sūta said:
Therein, neither old age, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor the fear of death exists;
the cycle of the seasons does not occur, and no disease arises.
Always sinless in the world of Brahmā; indeed, for one who has gone to the world of Brahmā.
But when Kakudmin had departed for that world of Raivata, alas, that entire Kuśasthalī was seized by sinful people and Rākṣasas. || 36 ||
That virtuous and high-souled one had a hundred brothers;
being slaughtered by the Rākṣasas, they fled in all directions out of fear. || 37 ||
And as that hundred of brothers fled, O best of Brahmins,
those Kṣatriyas there and then were indeed overcome by fear of them.
But there, O best of the twice-born, their lineages were exceedingly great in various places. || 38 ||
For those to whom these best of sages,
renowned as the Śāryātas,
were kṣatriyas endowed with excellent qualities.
Renowned in all directions. || 39 ||
Those of great power have entered every thicket in every way;
they are the two sons of Nabhaga and Ariṣṭa.
Two Vaiśyas attained the status of Brāhmaṇas. || 40 ||
From Karūṣa came the Kārūṣas, Kṣatriyas fierce in battle,
who were renowned as the Śāryātas.
In all directions, there were those who were righteous. || 39 ||
All the boldness of Dhṛṣṭa was displayed in battle;
indeed, he led a host of three thousand.
Of the high-souled Kṣatriyas. || 40 ||
And the heir of Nābhaga was the powerful one named Nābhāga; for Pṛṣadhra, having committed violence—
O best of the twice-born, [they gave] a cow to their guru. || 41 ||
Having fallen into the state of a Śūdra due to a curse,
these nine are proclaimed as the sons of Vaivasvata.
Indeed, O best of sages, [this was] for Manu. || 42 ||
Ambarīśa was the son of Nābhāgi, and Virūpa was his son. || 41 ||
Pr̥ṣadaśva was the son of Virūpa;
his son was Rathītara.
These were indeed born of the Kṣatriya lineage.
Furthermore, they are remembered as Aṅgirases;
they are the Rathītaras, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas. || 42 ||
Formerly, as Manu was sneezing, Ikṣvāku became his son;
that Ikṣvāku had a hundred sons who gave profuse sacrificial fees.
Among them, the eldest was Vikukṣi;
because of his lack of appetite (vikukṣitva),
he attained Ayodhyā, they being knowers of the supreme Dharma.
He was the lord and sovereign of Ayodhyā.
Among them, there were three: Vikukṣi, Nimi, and Daṇḍa, of whom Vikukṣi was the eldest.
It is recorded that he had five hundred sons, with Śakuni as their leader.
There were forty-eight kings who were the protectors of the land of the Northern Path, and likewise [eight] in the southern direction. || 45 ||
Vaśati and the others were appointed as protectors of the southern region. Then, on the occasion of the Aṣṭakā festival, Ikṣvāku indeed commanded Vikukṣi: || 46 ||
"O mighty one, having slain deer, bring meat for the sake of the śrāddha;
it has been designated for the śrāddha rite, yet the śrāddha rite remains unperformed! (47)
O Brahmins, at the command of that wise one,
having slain thousands of deer and having eaten the hare, he departed.
Śāśāda went out on a hunt. || 48 ||
When Viśvāmitra had arrived with his army and his attendants, he urged Vasiṣṭha, saying, "Let meat be sprinkled for the sacrifice. || 48 ||
Having been thus commanded by the king, he approached according to the prescribed rites;
seeing that the meat was spoiled, he became enraged and spoke to the king: || 48 ||
O King, this meat has been defiled by a low-born person—by your own son—and because it was eaten by a hare, this meat of yours is indeed unfit to be consumed, O one of great luster. (48)
O sinless one, O best of kings, that hare was previously devoured by a wicked-souled being in the forest; therefore, this meat is unfit for the ancestors. (48)
Then Ikṣvāku, enraged, said this to Vikuṣi:
"You were appointed by me for the ancestral rites, yet you have gone hunting."
"O pitiless one, you previously ate hares in the forest, but today [you eat me];
therefore, I abandon you—go by your own karma! || 48 ||
The lord was abandoned by Ikṣvāku at the word of Vasiṣṭha; when Ikṣvāku had passed away, the brahmin [remained].
But Śaśāda became the king. || 49 ||
Having attained that supreme state, he became the lord of Ayodhyā;
urged by Vasiṣṭha, he indeed ruled the kingdom. || 49 ||
Then, filled with that sin while in the state of ruling the kingdom, the lord of the earth passed away in due time and went to an even lower state of existence.
Having understood this narrative, one should certainly not eat meat according to improper rules;
for he who eats my flesh here shall be eaten by me in the next world.
The wise declare this to be the "meat-ness" of meat. The heir of Śāśāda was the powerful one named Kakutstha. || 50 ||
From Indra, who had become a bull, Kakutstha was born; because he defeated the Asuras in the former battle at Āḍīvakā, he is remembered as Kakutstha. || 51 ||
From Anenas, Kakutstha was born; Pṛthu is recorded as the son of Anenas.
Viṣṭarāśva was the son of Pṛthu, and from him Ārdra was born. || 52 ||
The son of Ārdra was Yuvanāśva, and his son was Śrāvasta;
from him was born King Śrāvastaka, by whom the city of Śrāvastī was founded. || 53 ||
The heir of Śrāvasta was the lord of the earth Bṛhadaśva;
his son was Kuvalāśva, a king most righteous. || 54 ||
He was the king who, because of the slaying of Dhundhu, attained the title of Dhundhumāra. || 55 ||
The sages said:
O highly wise one, we wish to hear in truth the account of Dhundhu’s slaughter, and for what purpose Kuvalāśva attained the status of Dhundhumāra. || 56 ||
Sūta (Lomaharṣaṇa) said: Kuvalāśva had a hundred sons,
all of whom were excellent archers, proficient in the sciences, powerful, and difficult to overcome.
All were righteous, performers of sacrifices, and givers of abundant sacrificial fees.
Bṛhadaśva, his father, installed Kuvalāśva in the kingdom. || 58 ||
Bṛhadaśva consecrated that Kuvalāśva, who was of great heroism, brave, and supremely righteous.
In that kingdom, there was a lord of men. || 58 ||
Having transferred his royal fortune to his son, the king indeed entered the forest;
then the brahmin-sage Uttāṅka restrained him as he was departing. || 59 ||
But the brahmin seer Uttāṅka restrained him as he was departing. || 59 ||
Uttāṅka said:
"Protection must be provided by you; therefore, you ought to do so for now.
For I am unable, O King, to practice penance free from anxiety. (60)
Indeed, near my hermitage, in the level desert lands, there is a sea filled with sand known as Ujjānaka. || 61 ||
Invulnerable to the gods, possessing a massive body and great strength,
that great being dwelt there within the earth, hidden beneath the sands.
The great asura named Dhundhu, the son of the Rākṣasa Madhu, lies performing severe penance for the destruction of the world. || 63 ||
At the end of each year, he would release a sigh;
whenever that occurred, the earth, together with its forests, trembled there. || 64 ||
By the wind of his breath, a great cloud of dust is raised,
obscuring the path of the sun for seven days, accompanied by an earthquake.
"O King, it was accompanied by sparks, embers, and smoke, and was exceedingly terrible;
because of that, I am unable to remain in my own hermitage. || 66 ||
"Slay him, O mighty-armed one, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds!
Once he has been struck down by you today, the worlds will become at peace. (67)
For you alone, O lord of the earth, are capable of slaying him;
moreover, O sinless one, a boon was granted to me by Viṣṇu in a former age. (68)
To him who shall slay that fierce and mighty great asura, you [shall grant] by means of the granting of a boon.
You shall cause the splendor to increase.
For Dhundhu, who possesses great heroism, cannot be overcome by a small amount of splendor;
Viṣṇu will augment your own immense splendor with his own. || 69 ||
O protector of the earth, it cannot be consumed even by divine rains for a hundred years. || 70 ||
For his vigor is truly immense, difficult to overcome even by the gods. || 71 ||
Thus addressed by the high-souled Uttāṅka,
that royal seer Bṛhadaśva gave his son Kuvalāśva to him for the purpose of slaying Dhundhu. || 72 ||
"O Blessed One, I have laid down my weapons; however, this son of mine, O best of the twice-born, will become Dhundhumāra, of this there is no doubt. || 73 ||
Having thus commanded his son for the slaying of Dhundhu, that royal seer of rigid vows departed for the mountains to practice asceticism.
But the righteous King Kuvalāśva, together with his hundred sons— Kuvalāśva, indeed, was a virtuous soul— [set forth].
Relying on his father’s word,
that king, together with twenty-one thousand sons, [set out].
Accompanied by Uttāṅka, he set out for the destruction of that Dhundhu.
Then the Lord, the blessed Viṣṇu, entered him with his splendor at the command of Uttāṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. || 76 ||
As that invincible one set forth, a great sound arose in the sky:
"This illustrious one shall today become the slayer of Dhundhu, the Unslayable! (77)
The gods scattered divine garlands all around him, and the celestial drums resounded loudly at that time. || 78 ||
Having gone there with his sons, that heroic one, the best among victors, caused the inexhaustible ocean filled with sand to be dug up. || 79 ||
Sustained by the splendor of Nārāyaṇa, that brahmin seer became possessed of great majesty and was further endowed with strength. || 80 ||
Then, as his sons were digging, Dhundhu, who was hidden beneath the sand,
was discovered there while stationed toward the western direction.
As if overturning the worlds with the fire born from his mouth out of anger,
he emitted water with great force, like the great ocean at the time of the moon's rising.
Of Soma; that great and best of Asuras was turbulent with streams of fluid.
His hundred sons, less three, were consumed by the Rākṣasa. || 82 ||
Then that radiant king, possessed of great splendor and the destroyer of Dhundhu, encountered the immensely powerful Rākṣasa Dhundhu.
That lord of the Urasas drank up his watery torrent;
and as a yogin, he extinguished the fire with water through the power of yoga.
Having slain that water-demon of massive body by force, the king, his task accomplished, displayed Uttanka. || 86 ||
Uttāṅka, however, granted a boon to that high-souled king:
he gave him inexhaustible wealth and invincibility against his enemies.
May there be constant delight in the Dharma and likewise an imperishable residence in heaven;
and may the sons who were slain by the Rākṣasa attain imperishable worlds in heaven. || 88 ||
Three of his sons remained; Dṛḍhāśva is said to be the eldest, while Candrāśva and Kapilāśva were the two younger princes. || 89 ||
Dhundhumāri and Dṛḍhāśva were born, and Haryaśva was his son;
Nikumbha was the son of Haryaśva, who was always devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya. || 90 ||
Samhatāśva, the son of Nikumbha, was skilled in battle;
both Akṛśāśva and Kṛśāśva were the two sons of Samhatāśva. || 91 ||
His daughter was Dṛṣadvatī, the daughter of Himavat, the mother of the virtuous;
she is renowned throughout the three worlds, and her son was Prasenajit. || 92 ||
Prasenaḍit obtained a wife named Gaurī, who was devoted to her husband;
however, having been falsely accused by her husband, she indeed became the Bāhudā river. || 93 ||
Her son was the great lord of the earth, Yuvanāśva;
and Māndhātṛ was the son of Yuvanāśva, the conqueror of the three worlds. || 94 ||
Regarding this, the twice-born reciters of the Purāṇas cite these verses:
"From where the sun rises until where it sets, all that is called the domain of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva. (94)
Caitrarathī, the daughter of Śaśabindu, became his wife;
she was a virtuous woman named Bindumatī, peerless on earth in her beauty. (95)
She was devoted to her husband and was the eldest of ten thousand brothers.
Upon her, Māndhātṛ then begot two sons. || 96 ||
Purukutsa, who was knowledgeable in dharma, and Mucukunda, who was righteous;
and the other son of Ambarīṣa is remembered as Yuvanāśva. || 96 ||
Harita was the son of Yuvanāśva, and from him the Hāritas are said to have descended;
for these were the sons of Aṅgiras, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas. Trasadasyu, however, was the son of Purukutsa and a lord of the earth.
He was born from the Narmadā, and Saṃbhūta was his son. The son of Saṃbhūta was indeed the powerful Anaraṇya. || 98 ||
He who was formerly slain by Rāvaṇa during the conquest of the three worlds was Trasadaśva, the son of Anaraṇya; and Haryaśva was his son.
From Haryaśva, by Dṛṣadvatī, was born King Vasumanas. The heir of Saṃbhūta was his son, King Tridhanvan, the crusher of enemies; he was a righteous man named Tridhanvan. || 98 ||
King Tridhanvan had a wise and powerful lord named Trayyāruṇa;
he had a son, a prince of great strength named Satyavrata. || 99 ||
Regarding the mantras of the taking of the hand:

by him, that evil-minded one, a wife was made an obstacle for Vidarbha; having slain the dwellers of heaven, she was carried off—she by whom a wife had previously been carried off during the mantras of the taking of the hand.
Having indeed performed the marriage for another, they have reached their final conclusion here.
Out of childishness, desire, delusion, exultation, and fickleness,
he carried off the maiden out of passion.
Of a certain resident of the city. || 100 ||
Filled with anger and repeatedly crying out, "Begone!", Trayyāruṇa abandoned him because of that stake of unrighteousness. || 102 ||
Abandoned, he said repeatedly to his father, "Where shall I go?
Then the father spoke to him: "Live together with the outcasts. || 103 ||
"I do not desire a son through you as my son, O defiler of the family!"—having been addressed thus by his father's words, he departed from the city. || 104 ||
But the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him;
that wise Satyavrata, however, [dwelt] near the dwellings of the outcaste dog-cookers.
Abandoned by his father, the hero lived on, while his father departed for the forest;
thereafter, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain upon that realm.
At that time, by means of that dharma, twelve years were indeed completed.
[Viṣṇuvṛddha was his son,
from whom the Viṣṇuvṛddhas are traditionally known.]
Out of desire, force, delusion, and through exhilaration and power,
as well as by the power of a future event.
That was accomplished by that wise one. || 101 ||
His father, Trayyāruṇa, abandoned him because he was joined with unrighteousness;
however, the great ascetic Viśvāmitra took his wife into his own domain.
Having renounced the world, he practiced intense penance on the shore of the ocean.
His wife, having bound her own middle son, her biological offspring, around his neck, [followed him]. (108)
He indeed sold him for a hundred cows for the sake of supporting his remaining family;
but seeing him bound by the neck for the purpose of sale, the prince—
The righteous and firm-vowed Satyavrata, the mighty-armed one, liberated the son of the great ṛṣi and took upon himself the responsibility for his maintenance.
For the sake of Viśvāmitra’s satisfaction and out of compassion alone,
that great ascetic and wise Kauśika Ṛṣi, who had been bound by a noose around his neck, became known as Gālava after being liberated by that hero. || 111 ||
## Section 4. Vaṃśānucarita | Chapter 2. B.
But Satyavrata, remaining steadfast in discipline, supported the wife of Viśvāmitra out of devotion, compassion, and his promise. || 1 ||
Having killed deer, boars, and wild buffaloes, he tied the meat to a tree in the vicinity of Viśvāmitra’s hermitage. || 2 ||
Having undertaken a twelve-year initiation with a vow of silence,
he lived out his father’s command while the king had gone to the forest.
And the sage Vasiṣṭha protected Ayodhyā, the kingdom, and likewise the inner apartments, by virtue of his relationship as both sacrificial priest and preceptor. || 4 ||
But Satyavrata, due to his youth and the power of destiny, constantly harbored an excessive resentment toward Vasiṣṭha. || 5 ||
For at that time, the sage Vasiṣṭha did not prevent his own son from being banished from the kingdom by his father, for there was a specific reason for this.
The completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the seventh step;
therefore, Satyavrata did not take her hand at the seventh step. || 7 ||
"O twice-born ones, Satyavrata then became enraged, thinking, 'Though Vasiṣṭha knows all dharmas, he does not protect me.'"
He set his mind upon Vasiṣṭha. || 8 ||
Out of regard for his virtue, the venerable Vasiṣṭha acted in that manner;
however, Satyavrata did not perceive that [act] of his as being in secret. || 9 ||
Because of the dissatisfaction that the high-souled father felt toward him,
Pākaśāsana did not send rain for twelve years.
The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha did not dissuade him from abandoning his father; for the sage’s mind was resolved thus: "I shall consecrate this son of his. || 12 ||
The powerful one, however, observed that initiation for twelve years;
meanwhile, meat was unavailable for the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
That prince beheld the cow who milks all desires;
indeed, he was possessed by anger, delusion, fatigue, and hunger. (14)
The king who had attained the ten dharmas slew the best of sages;
he himself ate the meat, as did the sons of Viśvāmitra. (15)
He caused [them] to be fed; having heard that, Vasiṣṭha also became enraged at him.
But the venerable one, being angry, spoke these words, and the venerable Vasiṣṭha said this to the son of the king: || 16 || Vasiṣṭha said to that son of the king: || 16 ||

"O cruel one, I would undoubtedly cause you to fall [into hell], were it not for these two stakes of yours; were there not three stakes of yours, they would surely be dug out again, O lowest of men. (17)

"Because of your father's dissatisfaction, because of the killing of your teacher's milch cow, and because of your consumption of meat not consecrated by sprinkling—these are your three transgressions. || 18 ||
Having seen those three pegs of his in this way, the one of great asceticism said, "Triśaṅku";
for that reason, he is remembered as Triśaṅku. || 19 ||
Viśvāmitra, however, having been approached for the sake of maintaining his wives, the pleased sage granted a boon to Triśaṅku. || 20 ||
Then, being invited to choose a boon, the prince chose this boon:
"May I go to heaven in my physical body"—thus was the boon requested. || 21 ||
When that twelve-year period of fear caused by drought had passed,
the sage consecrated him in his paternal kingdom and then performed a sacrifice for him.
While the deities and Vasiṣṭha were looking on, the lord Kauśika then indeed caused him to ascend to heaven in his physical body. || 23 ||
His wife, named Satyarathā, born of the Kaikeya lineage, gave birth to a sinless prince, Hariścandra. || 24 ||
That King Hariścandra is indeed remembered as Traiśaṅkava;
he was renowned as a sovereign emperor (samrāṭ) who performed the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 25 ||
The son of Hariścandra was the heroic one named Rohita; Harita was the son of Rohita, and Cañcu is said to be the son of Hārīta. || 26 ||
Vijaya and Sudeva became the two sons of Cañcu;
because he was the conqueror of all the kṣatriyas, he was remembered as Vijaya. || 27 ||
Ruruka was his son, a king skilled in the knowledge of dharma and artha;
Vṛka was the son of Ruruka, and from Vṛka, Bāhu was born. || 28 ||
The Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas drove that king out; the king was expelled, being addicted to vice. His wife, carrying the fetus, departed.
He entered the hermitage of Aurva. || 29 ||
And he was exceedingly righteous, for he lived in the Age of Dharma (Kṛtayuga).
Sagara was indeed born as the son of Bāhu, along with the poison (gara). || 30 ||
Having reached the hermitage of Aurva and being protected by Bhārgava,
King Sagara received the Āgneya weapon from Bhārgava.
Having slain the Tālajaṅghas along with the Haihayas, he conquered the earth;
the infallible one then abolished the religious practices of the Śakas and the Pahlavas.
Likewise, he who knows the dharma [spoke] regarding those Kṣatriyas and the Pāradas. || 33 ||
The sages said:
How was that Sagara born as one possessed of poison (gara), O Acyuta?
And for what reason [was he born] among the Kṣatriyas of great power, such as Śakra and the others?
In his anger, King Acyuta cast aside the duties appropriate to his lineage;
O high-minded one, relate all of this to us in detail! (35)

Sūta (Lomaharṣaṇa) said: "It is said that in former times, the kingdom of Bāhu was seized while he was distracted by his vices, after he had encountered the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas, and the Śakas. || 36 ||
The Yavanas, the Pāradas, the Kāmbojas, and likewise the Pahlavas—
these five tribes indeed exerted their prowess for the sake of the Haihayas. || 37 ||
Then that king Bāhu, having been deprived of his kingdom, went to the forest,
followed by his wife, in great sorrow.
He gave up his life in the forest. || 38 ||
His Yādava wife, however, followed behind him while pregnant;
it is said that poison had previously been administered to her by a co-wife. || 39 ||
Having prepared her husband's funeral pyre in the forest, she ascended it;
but Aurva Bhārgava, seeing her, restrained her out of compassion. || 40 ||
And in his hermitage, that mighty-armed one was born from the womb together with the poison itself, O Acyuta.
There was a king named Sagara. || 41 ||
But Aurva, having performed for that great-souled one the birth-rites and other ceremonies,
and having taught him the Vedas and the Shastras, then imparted to him the divine weapons.
The mighty-armed one [Rāma], endowed with both the power of that weapon and his own strength, [faced] that which was unbearable even for the immortals. || 43 ||
Enraged like Rudra slaughtering sacrificial animals, he swiftly destroyed the Haihayas;
that best among the famous acquired fame throughout the worlds. || 44 ||
Then the king resolved to exterminate the Śakas, the Yavanas, the Kāmbojas, the Pāradas, and the Pahlavas without leaving a remnant. || 45 ||
Being slaughtered by the heroic and high-souled Sagara,
those wise ones sought refuge with Vasiṣṭha and prostrated before the sage.
But Vasiṣṭha, of great splendor, seeing them, then granted them safety and restrained Sagara by means of an agreement. || 47 ||
Having heard his own promise and the words of his preceptor, Sagara indeed destroyed their dharma and caused them to change their appearance. || 48 ||
Having shaved half the heads of the Śakas, he let them go;
likewise, he shaved the entire heads of the Yavanas and the Kāmbojas. || 49 ||
By that great-souled one, the Pāradas were made to have disheveled hair, the Pahlavas to grow beards, and [all] were deprived of the study of the Vedas and the utterance of the vaṣaṭ-call. || 50 ||
The Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and likewise the Pahlavas; the Kolisarpas along with the Mahiṣas, the Dārvas, the Colas, and the Keralas. || 51 ||
All those groups of Kṣatriyas had their dharma abolished by the high-souled King Sagara, acting upon the word of Vasiṣṭha. || 52 ||
That king, victorious through righteousness, having conquered this earth, released a horse while consecrated for the horse sacrifice (vājimedha). || 53 ||
As he was leading him, that horse was carried away near the shore in the south-eastern ocean and made to enter the earth. || 54 ||
Then that king had that region excavated by his sons.
While that great ocean was being dug up, they arrived there. (55)
[He saw] that primordial Person, the God Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Creatures, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Puruṣa, sleeping in the form of Kapila. || 56 ||
As he was awakening, all his sons were consumed by the radiance arising from his eyes; however, four remained as survivors. || 57 ||
Barhiketu, Suketu, and likewise King Dharmaratha, as well as the heroic Pañcajana—these were the kings who perpetuated his lineage. || 58 ||
And the Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa granted him boons:
an imperishable lineage for Ikṣvāku and an undying fame. (59)
The Lord granted his son and the ocean an imperishable residence in heaven;
and the ocean, taking the goat, [departed].
He paid homage to that lord of the earth.
The imperishability of his own lineage, as well as a hundred horse-sacrifices. || 59 ||
The Lord [granted] a son and the ocean,
as well as imperishable residence in heaven;
that ocean, taking the horse, [departed].
The lord of rivers paid his respects. || 60 ||
And by that very deed, he indeed attained the state of being the ocean;
and he recovered from the ocean that horse belonging to the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
That highly illustrious king performed a hundred horse-sacrifices;
we have heard that he had sixty thousand sons. || 62 ||
The sages said:
"How were the heroic sons of Sagara born, so exceedingly powerful? By what rite were those sixty thousand valiant ones produced? Tell us! (63)
Sūta (Lomaharṣaṇa) said: Sagara had two wives whose sins were burnt away by ascetic penance;
the elder was the daughter of Vidarbha, known by the name Keśinī.
But his youngest wife was most virtuous, the daughter of Ariṣṭanemi, peerless on earth in her beauty. || 65 ||
The lord Aurva, gratified by their ascetic penance, granted them a boon:
"Let one of these two ascetic women take sixty thousand sons. || 66 ||
"Let one of them choose as many sons as she desires from this single lineage-holder. Thereupon, one of them chose sons.
Likewise, greedy people [despise] many heroes. || 67 ||
"One shall be the bearer of the lineage," the Great Sage replied, "so be it.
Keśinī gave birth [to one] from Sagara.
From Asamañjas was born a son named Pañcajana; he was a king of great strength. || 68 ||
The sacred tradition states that the other [wife] gave birth to a gourd filled with seeds;
therein were sixty thousand [beings].
Your embryos are the size of sesame seeds. || 69 ||
One shall give birth to a desired son who will perpetuate the lineage;
[the other] shall give birth to sixty thousand sons.
The second [mother] gives birth. || 66 ||
Having heard the words of the sage,
Keśinī, the most excellent woman, [sought] her only son for the sake of the lineage.
He took it in the assembly of kings. || 67 ||
Likewise, the highly fortunate Suparṇabhaginī gave birth to sixty thousand sons,
who were exceedingly joyful.
Sumati likewise took hold [of it]. || 67 ||
Then, after some time had passed, Jyeṣṭhā gave birth to an eldest son known as Asamañja.
The descendant of Kakutstha, the son of Sagara.
The illustrious Sumati likewise conceived a gourd-like womb,
from which sixty thousand sons were born.
They have emerged from the middle of the gourd. || 69 ||
They came into being at the proper time and grew up in due order;
then, he placed those embryos in jars filled with clarified butter. || 70 ||
The king provided that many nurses, one for each [child], for their nourishment;
then, after ten months, they emerged comfortably.
Those princes, who increased the joy of Sagara, were sixty thousand sons born in due time.
O twice-born ones, such thoughts occurred to him.
Born from the womb, indeed from the interior of a gourd, of that lord of the earth;
of them, the splendor was Nārāyaṇa.
Of those great-souled ones who have entered [there]. || 73 ||
One son named Pañcajana indeed became a king;
the son of Pañcajana was...
The valiant one named Aṃśumān. || 74 ||
Those highly fortunate princes, who increased the joy of Sagara,
[lived] for a very long time.
They attained youth. || 72 ||
There were sixty thousand sons; among them, he was the eldest, a tiger among men, who followed after the horse.
The self-born son of Sagara.
The one known as Asamañja,
of great strength and with a peacock banner, was his son; Dilīpa was his son.
He was renowned as Khaṭvāṅga,
who, having come here from heaven and obtained life for but a moment, [performed this]. (74)
Three worlds, free from affliction,
were encompassed by the intellect and truth of Dilīpa’s heir.
The great king Bhagīratha. || 75 ||
He who was the lord that brought down the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers,
and led her to the ocean.
He even conceived of her as his daughter. || 76 ||
Therefore, she is called Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā by those who trace their lineages.
King Śruta was renowned as the son of Bhagīratha. || 77 ||
Devoted to the harm of the citizens,
he was banished from the city by his father;
his son was named Aṃśumān.
The heroic son of Asamañja. || 74 ||
His son was the righteous-souled one renowned as Dilīpa;
from Dilīpa [was born] the one of great splendor.
The heroic Bhagīratha was born. || 75 ||
By whom, indeed, the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers,
adorned with celestial chariots,
was brought here by the Lord of the Gods.
And she was conceived as his daughter. || 76 ||
Regarding this, the people who recite the Purāṇas cite this verse:
"Bhagīratha, however, [brought] that Gaṅgā..."
He brought [them] by means of his ritual acts. || 76 ||
And the son of Bhagīratha was indeed Śruta by name. || 77 ||
Nābhāga was the son of Śrutashravas, a most righteous man;
from Nābhāga came Ambarīṣa, and from him Sindhudvīpa was born. || 78 ||
Thus it is heard that those learned in the chronicles of old sing:
"Protected by the two arms of Ambarīṣa, the earth became free from the three types of suffering for the sake of its inhabitants. (78)
The valiant Ayutajit was the heir of Sindhudvīpa; Ayutajit’s son, moreover, was...
The highly illustrious Ṛtuparṇa.
Divyākṣa was indeed a knower of the heart, a friend of King Nala, and powerful;
he became the son of Ṛtuparṇa, the lord of the earth known as Ārtaparṇi. || 80 ||
His son was King Sudāsa, who was a friend of Indra;
the son of Sudāsa was the monarch named Saudāsa. || 81 ||
The one known as Kalmāṣapāda was indeed named Mitrasaha;
the son of Kalmāṣapāda was renowned as Sarvakarman. || 82 ||
Anaraṇya was the son of Viśruta Sarvakarman; Anaraṇya’s son was Nighna.
The two sons of Nighna were born. || 83 ||
Anamitra and Raghu were indeed the two most excellent among the bulls of kings;
the son of Anamitra was the king.
The wise man becomes one who milks the cow. || 84 ||
But Vasiṣṭha, of great splendor, [beheld him] in the field of Kalmāṣapādaka.
He begot Aśmaka for the sake of increasing the Ikṣvāku lineage;
he who was the legitimate son of Aśmaka—
Mūlaka was his son. || 83 ||
In this regard, they cite this example concerning King Mūlaka:
for that king, out of fear of Rāma, [acted as follows].
He lived surrounded by women. || 84 ||
Desiring protection while naked, the righteous-souled Lord indeed put on the armor of a woman made of radish.
King Śataratha is remembered [as such]. || 84 ||
From that Chataratha was born the powerful King Iḍāvida;
the illustrious Aiḍāvida was his son.
The powerful Kṛtaśarman [was there]. || 84 ||
Dilīpa was his son,
the great-grandfather of Rāma;
Dilīpa had long arms.
A son named Raghu was born. || 85 ||
In Ayodhyā, there was a great king named Raghu, possessed of mighty strength.
From Raghu, Aja was born.
In the same way, Daśaratha was also born. || 86 ||
Rāma, the righteous and highly illustrious son of Daśaratha,
having slain Mādhava Lavaṇa, went to that Madhuvana forest.
Śatrughna established the city of Mathurā there. || 861 ||
Subāhu and Śūrasena, both sons of Śatrughna, protected the city of Mathurā along with their two Vaideha wives. || 862 ||
Aṅgada and Candraketu were both the sons of Lakṣmaṇa;
their two prosperous provinces were situated near the Himavat mountains.
The city of Aṅgadīyā belongs to Aṅgada in the region of Kārapatha;
the auspicious city of Candravaktrā belongs to Mallaka, the son of Candraketu. || 864 ||
The two heroic sons of Bharata were Takṣa and Puṣkara;
the cities of those two high-souled ones were established in the region of Gāndhāra. (865)
The delightful city of Takṣaśilā is renowned in all directions for Takṣa;
likewise, Puṣkarāvatī is famous for the hero Puṣkara. || 866 ||
And on this matter, those people who are knowers of the ancient lore sing a verse concerning Rāma, which is grounded in truth and [arises] from the majesty of that wise one: || 867 ||

Dark-complexioned, youthful, with red eyes and a radiant face, he spoke with measured words; his arms reached down to his knees, his countenance was handsome, his shoulders were like those of a lion, and his arms were great.
Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years;
the sound of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas, along with the great resonance of the bowstring, [filled the air]. (869)
"Let it be given! Let it be enjoyed!"—thus it was proclaimed without interruption throughout the kingdom.
Dwelling in Janasthāna, he performed the work of the thirty gods. || 8610 ||
Seeking the tracks of Sītā, that bull among men of great renown first slew the descendant of Pulastya who had committed the offense. || 8611 ||
Endowed with courage, perfected in virtue, and blazing with his own splendor,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, shone forth surpassing both the sun and the fire.
Thus this mighty-armed lord, the delight of the Ikṣvāku clan,
having slain Rāvaṇa along with his host, ascended to heaven.
A son was born to Rāma, widely renowned as Kuśa. (87)
Kuśa was established in the kingdom of Kośala, and the delightful city of Kuśasthalī was founded by him upon the slopes of the Vindhya mountains. || 871 ||
The kingdom of Uttarakośala belongs to the high-souled Lava; Śrāvastī is world-renowned. Now learn of the lineage of Kuśa! || 872 ||
Atithi was born from Kuśa, and Niṣadha was his son;
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, and Nabha was the son of Nala.
From Nabhas came Puṇḍarīka, and from him Kṣemadhanvan is remembered. || 88 ||
The son of Kṣemadhanvan was the powerful Devānīka;
the lordly son of Devānīka was named Ahīnagu. || 89 ||
The heir of Ahīnagu was the king named Sudhanvan,
and Sudhanvan’s son was likewise [born].
From him was born King Śala. || 90 ||
That righteous-souled son of Śala was indeed named Uktha;
his son was Vajranābha.
And of the great-souled Uktha. || 91 ||
The learned son of Śaṅkhaṇa was known as Vyūṣitāśva;
and the son of Vyūṣitāśva was indeed King Viśvasaha. || 92 ||
His son was the learned Puṣya, and Dhruvasandhi was his son;
Sudarśana was his son, and from Sudarśana came Agnivarṇa. || 93 ||
The son of Agnivarṇa was Śīghra; the son of Śīghra was Maru.
Maru, however, having applied himself to yoga, settled in the village of Kalāpa. || 94 ||
In the nineteenth *yuga*, the lord who initiated the Kṣatriya lineage was Prasuśruta, the son of Maru;
Susaṃdhi was his son. || 94 ||
And from Susandhi was born the wrathful one known by the name Sahasvat;
the son of Sahasvat was the king named Viśrutavat. || 94 ||
The son of that renowned king was Bṛhadbala.
O best of sages, only two Nalas are renowned in the Purāṇas: Virasena and Ātmaja.
And he who was a scion of the Ikṣvāku lineage. || 95 ||
Those born of the Ikṣvāku lineage have been proclaimed primarily;
these [are] in the lineage of Vivasvat.
Kings of great splendor. || 96 ||
By correctly reciting this creation of the Sun, Vivasvat, the divine Śrāddhadeva, who bestows nourishment upon all creatures; 97.
Possessing offspring, he attains union with Vivasvat Āditya;
moreover, he becomes free from evil, free from passion, and long-lived. || 98 ||
Sūta said: Now learn of the lineage of Nimi, the younger brother of Vikukṣi,
who established that city which was like the supreme city of the gods.
It was known as Jayanta, situated near the hermitage of Gautama; in his lineage was indeed born Janaka, the best of kings. || 982 ||
O Great King, there was a son of Ikṣvāku, who possessed vast splendor, named Nimi; he was a man of virtuous nature and was honored by all living beings. || 983 ||
By the curse of Vasiṣṭha, he became bodiless (videha);
his son, named Mithi, was born from three joints (parvan).
While the fire-drill was being rubbed in the forest, the one of great fame appeared;
he became known by the name Mithi, and from his birth, he was called Janaka. || 985 ||
There was one of great heroism named Mithi, from whom that city of Mithilā derived its name; he was the king known as Janaka, and from Janaka came Udāvasu. || 986 ||
From Udāvasu was born that righteous Nandivardhana;
from Nandivardhana came the virtuous Śūra, named Suketu. || 987 ||
The son of Suketu was the righteous and mighty Devarāta;
the son of Devarāta was known as the righteous Bṛhaduktha. || 988 ||
The son of Bṛhaduktha was the powerful and renowned Mahāvīrya;
Dhṛtimān was the son of Mahāvīrya, and Sudhṛti was his offspring. || 989 ||
The son of Sudhṛti was the righteous Dhṛṣṭaketu, a scorcher of enemies;
and the son of Dhṛṣṭaketu was the renowned Haryaśva.
Maru was the son of Haryaśva, and Pratiṃbaka was the son of Maru.
The righteous King Kīrtiratha is remembered as the son of Pratiṃbaka. || 9811 ||
The son of Kīrtiratha was known as Devamīḍha;
the son of Devamīḍha was Vibudha, and the son of Vibudha was Mahādhṛti.
The son of Mahādhṛti was the powerful King Kīrtirāta;
the son of Kīrtirāta was the learned one renowned as Mahāroma. || 9813 ||
From Mahāromā was born the famous Svarṇaroman;
and the son of Svarṇaroman was King Hrasvaroman.
The learned son of Hrasvaroman was known as Sīradhvaja, by whom the illustrious furrow (sītā) was ploughed;
she who became the virtuous queen of Rāma, faithful to her vows and exceedingly devoted to her husband. || 9815 ||
Vaiśampāyana (Śāṃśapāyana) said:
How was the illustrious Sītā produced while the field was being ploughed? And for what purpose did the king plough the field in which she came into being? || 9816 ||
Sūta said:
While the sacrificial ground for the Horse Sacrifice of that great-souled one was being ploughed according to the well-applied ritual, she indeed arose from it. || 9817 ||
The younger brother of Sīradhvaja was the Mithilā king named Bhānumān;
his brother was Kuśadhvaja, who was the sovereign of Kāśī.
The son of that Bhānumat was the powerful Pradyumna;
his son was Muni, and from him Ūrjavaha is said to have descended.
From Ūrjavāha was born Sanadvāja, and Śakuni was his son;
Svāgata was the son of Śakuni, and Suvarcas is recorded as his offspring. || 9820 ||
Śruta was his heir, and Suśruta was his son;
Jaya was the son of Śuśruta, and Vijaya was the son of Jaya.
Vijaya’s son was Ṛta; Ṛta’s son is remembered as Sunaya;
from Sunaya came Vītahavya, and Vītahavya’s son was Dhṛti. || 9822 ||
From Dhṛti was born Bahulāśva, and the son of Bahulāśva was Kṛti;
with him the lineage of the high-souled Janakas comes to an end.
Thus have these Maithilas been described; now learn also of Soma! || 9823 ||
## Section 4. Vaṃśānucarita | Chapter 3 | A.
O Brahmins, the venerable sage Atri was born as the father of Soma from the mind of Brahmā in the beginning.
Desiring to bring about the creation of progeny.
There Atri remained, surrounded by his sons, performing only auspicious deeds through action, mind, and speech;
that one of great splendor stood with arms upraised, as motionless as wood, a wall, or a stone. || 2 ||
There was an unsurpassed austerity which he practiced in the past;
indeed, we have heard that it lasted for three thousand divine years. || 3 ||
O twice-born one, as that great being of perpetual celibacy remained there with unblinking eyes, his body indeed attained the state of the moon.
As his self was thus purified, his essence ascended upward;
from his two eyes flowed water, illuminating the ten directions. || 5 ||
Then, commanded by the prescribed rite, ten goddesses took up that embryo;
they held it together, yet they were unable to sustain it individually. || 6 ||
Then, from those directions, that radiant embryo suddenly fell, illuminating the worlds like the moon, the benefactor of all beings. || 7 ||
When those quarters of space were no longer able to sustain that embryo, it then fell swiftly to the earth along with them. || 8 ||
Beholding Soma fallen, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, placed him upon his chariot out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. || 9 ||
For he, O brahmins, is composed of the Vedas, righteous-souled, and true to his promise;
we have heard that he is yoked to a thousand white horses. || 10 ||
When that son of Atri, the Supreme Soul, had descended, the seven renowned mind-born sons of Brahmā, the gods, offered hymns of praise. || 11 ||
Right there were the sons of that Aṅgiras and likewise those of Bhṛgu, with Ṛks, Yajus, Sāmans, and also the Atharvāṅgirases. || 12 ||
As he was being thus praised, the splendor of that radiant Soma caused the three worlds to swell and nourish them on all sides.
With that preeminent chariot, he of exceeding fame circumambulated the earth bounded by the oceans twenty-one times. || 14 ||
That splendor of his which was displaced fell upon the earth;
from it the plants arose, blazing indeed with that splendor. || 15 ||
By them the three worlds and the fourfold progeny are to be sustained;
for the blessed Soma, O best of the twice-born, is the nourisher of the universe. || 16 ||
Having attained splendor through those praises and those deeds, the illustrious and highly fortunate Blessed One performed ascetic penance for one hundred and twenty million years. 17.
The goddesses who are golden-hued and sustain the world by their own power—among them, Soma became preeminent through his own deed. || 18 ||
Then, O best of the twice-born, Brahmā, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, bestowed upon him sovereignty over seeds, medicinal herbs, brāhmaṇas, and waters. || 19 ||
Thus consecrated in the great sovereignty of a king of kings, that one of great splendor, the best among the radiant, illuminated the three worlds with his own brilliance. || 20 ||
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave twenty-seven daughters of great vows to Indu; they are known as the Nakṣatras. || 21 ||
Having obtained that great kingdom, Soma, the best among those who possess the moon,
performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, in which hundreds of thousands were given as sacrificial fees.
The venerable Atri was the Hotṛ priest of this [sacrifice], Bhṛgu became the Adhvaryu, Hiraṇyagarbha was the Udgātṛ, and Brahmā assumed the office of the Brahman priest. || 23 ||
The Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign, was present there as a member of the assembly, surrounded by the foremost ancient Brahman-sages headed by Sanatkumāra. || 24 ||
"O twice-born ones, we have heard that Soma gave the three worlds as a sacrificial fee to those chief Brahman-sages and to the members of the assembly. || 25 ||
Sinī, Kuhū, Dyuti, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, Vasu, Kīrti, Dhṛti, and Lakṣmī—these nine goddesses waited upon him. || 26 ||
Having completed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with composure, the king of kings, honored by all the gods and sages, shone resplendent, illuminating the ten directions in ten ways. || 27 ||
O brahmins, having obtained that sovereignty which is difficult to attain and praised by the sages, his mind wandered, struck by improper conduct and a lack of humility. || 28 ||
He indeed forcibly carried off Bṛhaspati’s illustrious wife named Tārā, disregarding all the sons of Aṅgiras. || 29 ||
Though he was entreated by the gods as well as by the celestial rishis,
he did not at that time release Tārā to that descendant of Aṅgiras.
Uśanas likewise took up the rear-guard of that descendant of Aṅgiras, for he was formerly the highly resplendent disciple of his father, Bṛhaspati. || 31 ||
Out of that affection for Bṛhaspati, the Lord Rudra took up his Ājagava bow and became the rear-guard protector for him.
By that high-souled one, the supreme weapon named Brahmaśiras was discharged against the gods, by which their glory was destroyed. || 33 ||
There, that great battle known as Tārakāmaya took place between the gods and the Dānavas, causing the destruction of the worlds. || 34 ||
Thereupon, those remaining gods who were known as the Tuṣitas went for refuge to Brahmā, the primordial and eternal deity. || 35 ||
Then, having restrained both Uśanas and Rudra Śaṅkara, the Grandfather himself gave Tārā back to Aṅgiras. || 36 ||
Seeing her with her time for delivery near at hand, and seeing that she was pregnant,
Bṛhaspati said to Tārā: "O Tārā, whose face is like the lord of stars,
you must by no means carry this fetus in my womb!"
Then he indeed created Tāra, that youth who is the greatest slayer of the Dasyus.
Having reached the stalk of the *iṣikā* grass, which was like a blazing fire, the Blessed One, as soon as he was born, eclipsed the bodies of the gods. || 39 ||
Then, fallen into doubt, those best of gods said to Tārā:
"Tell the truth; whose son is he—Soma’s or Bṛhaspati’s? (40)
When she did not say whether it was good or bad, even though she was questioned by the gods, the prince, the greatest slayer of robbers, then began to curse her. || 41 ||
Having restrained him, Brahmā then asked Tārā about his doubt:
"O Tārā, tell me what is the truth in this matter; whose son is this? (42)
With palms joined in reverence, she spoke thus to the Lord Brahmā, the granter of boons,
concerning the high-souled Soma’s son, the Kumāra who is the greatest slayer of the Dasyus.
Then King Soma, the Lord of Creatures, having smelled the head of his son, gave that wise son the name Budha. || 44 ||
And at that time, an unfavorable planet rose in the sky;
yet the princess gave birth to a son. (45)
His son was the highly resplendent Aila Purūravas. Seven sons were born to that great-souled one by Urvaśī; six sons of exceeding power were born to him by Urvaśī. || 46 ||
There, he was forcibly overpowered and rendered helpless by consumption;
then, overcome by consumption, Soma’s orb began to wane. || 47 ||
Then he went for refuge to his father, Atri himself.
The highly illustrious Atri performed that pacification of his sin;
freed from consumption, he blazed forth with splendor on all sides. || 48 ||
Thus has been proclaimed the birth of Soma, which increases one's fame;
O best of the twice-born, now learn of his lineage as it is being recited! (49)
Meritorious, conducive to health and long life, and the fulfillment of one's intentions—merely by hearing of the birth of Soma, one is liberated from sins. || 50 ||
## Section 4. Vaṃśānucarita | Chapter 3 | B.
O best of sages, the son of Budha was the learned Purūravas.
He was radiant, charitable by nature, a performer of sacrifices, and one who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
A proponent of Brahman, valiant, and invincible by enemies in battle,
he was a sovereign lord who maintained the sacred fire and performed sacrifices.
Truthful, virtuous-minded, handsome, and restrained in sexual conduct,
he became peerless in beauty throughout the three worlds.
The illustrious Urvaśī, casting aside her pride, chose him as her husband—he who was a teacher of the Veda, self-controlled, a knower of dharma, and a speaker of truth. || 4 ||
The valiant king lived with her for ten years and five, and for five, six, seven, eight, ten, and eight [years]. (5)
In the delightful Caitraratha forest, likewise on the banks of the Mandākinī,
in the vast city of Alakā, and in the Nandana, the best of groves.
Having reached the Northern Kurus,
where the trees grant the fruits of one's desires,
he stayed at the foot of Mount Gandhamādana and likewise upon the northern peak of Meru.
O King,
in these excellent forests frequented by the gods,
the king, accompanied by Urvaśī, took delight with supreme joy. || 8 ||
The sages said: (Janamejaya said: "O you who have heard much! Tell us how the divine Gandharvī Urvaśī, having abandoned the gods, came to a mortal king."
Sūta (Vaiśampāyana) said:
Terrified by the curse of Brahmā, she entered a human form;
that woman of beautiful hips approached Aila when the appointed time arrived.
For the sake of liberation from her own curse, she established this covenant:
"Not seeing fire, and engaging in sexual intercourse with one who has desire. (11)
At that time, two rams were tied up near his bed, O King, and his food consisted solely of ghee for a certain period of time. || 12 ||
"O King, if this agreement is firm for as long as you desire, then for that duration I shall dwell here; the agreement has indeed been made between us. (13)
The king observed all those conditions of hers;
thus did that noble lady dwell there with Purūravas.
For fifty-nine years, however, she remained attached to him, deluded by the curse.
While Urvashi was dwelling among humans, the Gandharvas were filled with anxiety: || 15 ||
The Gandharvas said:
"O highly fortunate ones, reflect upon how that excellent woman Urvaśī, the ornament of heaven, might once again come to the gods. (16)
Then Viśvāvasu, the best among speakers, said there:
"I previously heard the agreement being made between those two. (17)
I know in its entirety how she will indeed abandon the king by transgressing the established rule, and how that monarch will break it. || 18 ||
"I shall go with my companions for the sake of accomplishing your purpose.

That lord of the earth, possessed of great fame, established his kingdom at Prayāga on the northern bank of the Jāhnavī, in the city of Pratiṣṭhāna. || 47 ||
They became seven sons of Āli, resembling the sons of gods;
high-souled ones born in heaven.
Āyus, Dhīmat, and Amāvasu. || 48 ||
Viśvāyu, the righteous-souled Śrutāyu, as well as others— Dṛḍhāyu and Vanāyu.

The learned Suhotra was also of great strength;

He who performed the great sacrifice of the Sarvamedha, that grand rite,

Āyu, Dhīmat, and Amāvasu. || 48 ||

The king was then raised among the forest-dwellers along with the Pahlavas;

A powerful son equal to Indra. || 60 ||
"May I obtain [it]," he thought. Out of fear, Śakra approached him and recognized him;

Seeing her performing such exceedingly fierce penance, the thousand-eyed Purandara himself,

That Indra of the gods, the best of deities, conceived him as his own son;
he became King Gādhi.
Maghavan Kauśika himself. || 63 ||
The daughter of Purukutsa became his wife; Gādhi was born of her.

The lord Gādhi gave her to Ṛcīka, the son of Kāvya;

Invincible by the Kṣatriyas in this world, the slayer of the bulls among Kṣatriyas—
O auspicious lady, he shall likewise have for a son one who is steadfast and rich in asceticism.
"O best of the twice-born, this sacrificial pap shall produce one whose nature is tranquility.
Having spoken thus to his wife, Ṛcīka, the descendant of Bhṛgu, [departed]. (69)
Constantly devoted to asceticism, Gādhi entered the forest;
accompanied by his wife, he then went to the hermitage of Ṛcīka.
On the occasion of his pilgrimage to sacred fords, the lord of men went to see his daughter;
at that time, Satyavatī took two portions of sacrificial charu from the sage.

But the mother, by fate, gave her own *caru* to her daughter. || 72 ||
Out of ignorance, he then prepared the sacrificial pap for her, intended for himself;

She of terrible appearance held it with her blazing body;
then Ṛcīka, having seen her and pursued her through his yogic power, [acted].

Then that best of the twice-born said to his own wife of excellent complexion: "O blessed lady, you have been deceived by your mother through the cause of the exchange of the sacrificial porridge. || 75 ||
For your son will be born of cruel deeds and exceedingly terrible;

"For the entire universe, as Brahman, has been offered by me into him through ascetic fervor.

"O blessed lady, this desire was not intended by me to be so;
