Satyavatī spoke these words once more:
"O Sage, if you so desired, you could create even the worlds; how much more so a son! (80)
"You ought to grant me here a son whose nature is tranquility and who is upright;
O Lord, may I have a grandson of such a kind as this, and so too may you. (81)
"If this cannot indeed be done otherwise, O best of the twice-born," he then showed favor toward her by the power of her asceticism.
"O lady of excellent complexion, there is no distinction for me between my son and my grandson;

Formerly, due to a reversal of the sacrificial oblations (caru) for Bhr̥gu during a sacrifice to Rudra and Viṣṇu, and because he was born from the Vaiṣṇava portion of the fire, Jamadagni was born from the Vaiṣṇava fire. Jamadagni was born. || 85 || Jamadagni was born. || 85 ||

"The highly fortunate Kauśikī, the best of rivers, is well known.

He begot a son whose nature was asceticism, sacred knowledge, and tranquility;
he who, having attained equality with the Brahman-sages, became a Brahman-rishi himself. || 92 ||
But the righteous Viśvāmitra, known by the name Viśvaratha, was born through the grace of Bhṛgu from Kauśika as the increaser of the lineage. || 93 ||
It is said that Viśvāmitra’s son was Śunaḥśepha, who was indeed assigned to the state of a sacrificial animal at the sacrifice of Haridaśva. || 94 ||
Śunaḥśepha was indeed given back to Viśvāmitra by the gods;
because he was given by the gods (devaiḥ), he therefore became Devarāta. || 95 ||
And the sons of Viśvāmitra are recorded as Devarāta and others;
they are renowned throughout the three worlds, and their names follow hereafter: || 95 ||
There were the Devarātas and the Katiśas, from whom the Kātyāyanas are said to have descended.
From Śalāvatī, Hiraṇyākṣa was born; then Reṇu was born from Reṇukā.
Sāṃkṛti, Gālava, and the renowned Mudgala; Madhucchandas, Jaya, Devala, and likewise Aṣṭaka. || 96 ||
Kacchapa and Hārita were also the sons of Viśvāmitra;
the lineages of those high-souled Kauśikas are well known. || 97 ||
The Pāṇinas, the Babhruvas,
as well as the Dhyānajapyas,
the Pārthivas, and the Devarātas.
The Śālāṅkāyanas and the Bāṣkalas. || 98 ||
The Lohitas, the Yāmadūtas,

Likewise, there are other Saindhavāyanas. || 99 ||
The Devalas, the Reṇus, the Yājñavalkyas, the Samarṣaṇas, the Audumbaras, and the Abhiṣṇātās.
The Tārakāyaṇas and the Cuñculas. || 100 ||
The Śālāvatyas, the Hiraṇyākṣas, the Sāṃkṛtyas, the Gālavas, as well as Nārāyaṇi and another, Nara.
Of the wise Viśvāmitra. || 101 ||
O best of sages, many Kauśikas are recorded as having intermarried with other lineages of seers, including those of the Paurava clan.
And of the Brahman-sage Kauśika; || 102 ||
Furthermore, his connection with the lineage of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas in this family is well-known. || 102 ||
Those many Kauśikas who intermarry with other lineages of sages are thus remembered. || 101 ||
The Kauśikas, the Sauśrutas, and likewise the others, the Saindhavāyanas,
[are the descendants] of the meritorious Paurorava.
Of the Brahman-sage Kauśika. || 102 ||
Among the sons of Viśvāmitra, Śunaḥśepha is remembered as the eldest;
that best of sages, though born of Bhṛgu, indeed attained the status of a Kauśika. || 103 ||
And likewise, Aṣṭaka was the son of Viśvāmitra through Dṛṣadvatī;
the son of Aṣṭaka was Laubhya—thus the lineage of Jahnu has been described by me. || 104 ||
The sages said:
By what characteristic dharma, or by what austerity or sacred learning, was the status of a Brahmin attained here by kings such as Viśvāmitra and others? || 104 ||
By whatever designation the Kṣatriyas attained the status of Brāhmaṇas, we wish to know the distinction [between them] resulting from austerity as well as from gifts! || 104 ||
Thus addressed, he then spoke these meaningful words:
"One who desires righteousness and performs a sacrifice with wealth acquired through unjust means, having summoned the best of the twice-born, does not enjoy the fruit of that dharma. || 104 ||
And having adopted this very dharma, that evil-souled, lowest of men gives gifts to the Brahmins for the sake of deceiving the worlds. (104)
Having performed such intense recitation, yet unrestrained by greed for wealth and possessed of passion and delusion, he who finally gives [the merit] for the sake of purification— || 104 ||
The gifts given by that wicked-souled person, who is intent on violence though professing righteousness, become indeed fruitless. || 104 ||

Thus, for one who has acquired wealth through delusion and gives it away while performing sacrifices—such a person of evil soul, whose actions are defiled, finds that his gift does not endure. || 1047 ||
He bestows wealth acquired through righteous means upon those worthy of it;
and without being motivated by sensual desires, he performs sacrifices and gives gifts. || 1048 ||
He obtains the fruit of giving, and that gift brings about happiness;
through giving one obtains enjoyments, and through truth one goes to heaven. || 1049 ||
By means of austerity well-acquired through progeny, he stands having pervaded the worlds;
having pervaded them, that radiant one enjoys infinity within the worlds. || 10410 ||
Sacrifice is superior to giving, and austerity is superior to sacrifice;
truth is superior to austerity, and therefore knowledge is held to be the greatest. || 10411 ||
For it is heard that there were twice-born men endowed with the qualities of the Kṣatriya who attained perfection through austerity:
Viśvāmitra the king, Māndhātṛ, Saṃkṛti, and Kapi. || 10412 ||
Kāśya, Purukutsa, Śala, the lord Gṛtsamada, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Ajamīḍha, as well as Bhārgavyoma. || 10413 ||
Kākṣīvān, Auśija, King Śiśira, Rathāntara, Śaunaka, Viṣṇuvṛddha, and other kings likewise [attained it]. || 10414 ||
For these are remembered as being endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas, yet they attained the state of Ṛṣis through austerity;
all these royal seers (rājarṣis) have reached supreme perfection. || 10415 ||

The five sons of Āyu were likewise all heroes and great chariot-warriors.
And from Prabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu, kings were born. || 1 ||

There, the son of Kṣatravṛddha was the highly illustrious Sunahotra;

Kāśa and Śala—these two—and likewise the lord Gṛtsamada;

Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and likewise śūdras—

The Śaunakas and the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas were twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
Then there was Dīrghatapas, the son of King Kāśa, the lord of Kāśī; from Dīrghatapas came Dhanvan, and from him the learned Dhanvantari. || 6 ||
At the conclusion of his very great asceticism,

Sūta (Vaiśampāyana) said:
O twice-born ones, let this account of the birth of Dhanvantari be heard here!
He was born from the ocean in ancient times while it was being churned for the sake of the nectar of immortality. || 9 ||
Having previously arisen from the water-pot and being surrounded on all sides by splendor, he stood there indeed beholding Viṣṇu as he was practicing for the sake of attaining perfection. || 10 ||
"You are Abja! he said; therefore, he is remembered as Abja.
Abja spoke to Viṣṇu: "O Lord, I am indeed your son. || 11 ||
"O best of gods, grant me a portion and a place in your world!
Thus addressed, the Lord, seeing that it was the truth, spoke to him: (12)
For the distribution of the sacrifice was indeed performed of old by the gods worthy of sacrifice, and the ritual fire-offering was assigned among the deities by the great seers. || 13 ||
"It is not possible for me to perform a fire-oblation for you here at any time.
For you, O Lord of the Earth, have become inferior to the gods; indeed, you are their son. || 14 ||
In the second birth, however, you will attain renown in the world; even while remaining in the womb, you will possess the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*. || 15 ||
O Lord, with this very body you shall attain divinity;
the twice-born shall worship you with sacrificial porridges, mantras, vows, and recitations. || 16 ||
Furthermore, you shall divide Āyurveda into eight parts;
for this matter was necessarily destined to happen, as it was foreseen of old by the Lotus-born One.
"Upon reaching the second Dvāpara age, you shall become [the incarnation], of this there is no doubt.
Having granted him this boon, Viṣṇu vanished once again. || 18 ||
When the second Dvāpara age had arrived, that king of Kāśī, the son of Sunahotra,
as well as King Dīrghatapas, performed austerities out of a desire for sons.
"I shall take refuge in that deity who will grant me a son";
thus the king, desiring to propitiate the lotus-born god for the sake of a son, [spoke]. || 20 ||
Then the Blessed One, the Lotus-born, being pleased, invited him to choose a boon; Dhanvantari, gratified, spoke to the king. || 21 ||
"Whatever boon you desire, speak it; I shall grant that to you, O observer of noble vows! || 21 ||
The king said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, then become my son, renowned for his fame! Having granted permission with the words "So be it," he vanished right there. || 22 ||
Then, a god named Dhanvantari was born in his house;
he was the great king of Kāśī, the destroyer of all diseases. || 23 ||
Having received Ayurveda, along with its medical practices, from Bharadvāja, he divided it again into eight parts and imparted them to his disciples. || 24 ||
The sons of Dhanvantari were renowned as the Ketumāns; now, the son of Ketumān is remembered as the heroic Bhīmaratha. || 25 ||
The son of Bhīmaratha was also Divodāsa, a lord of subjects; he was born wise, a lord of subjects. Divodāsa, however, was righteous-souled and renowned as Divodāsa.
He became the sovereign of Vārāṇasī. || 26 || He became the sovereign of Vārāṇasī. || 26 ||
At that very time, however, a Rākṣasa named Kṣemaka caused the ancient city of Vārāṇasī to become deserted. || 27 ||
"For she has been cursed by the wise and great-souled Nikumbha:
'Without a doubt, you shall remain desolate for a thousand years! (28)"
As soon as she had been cursed, Divodāsa, the lord of subjects,
established a beautiful city on the Gomatī at the edge of his territory.
The sages said: (Janamejaya said:
For what reason did Nikumbha formerly curse Vārāṇasī? Who was this righteous-souled Nikumbha who cursed that field of perfection? || 30 ||
Sūta (Vaiśampāyana) said:
Having reached the city, O king, the royal seer Divodāsa, that lord of men possessed of great splendor, dwelt there in that prosperous city. || 31 ||
At that very time, O Great Lords, Maheśvara, having taken a wife and desiring to please the Goddess, lived in the presence of his father-in-law. || 32 ||
By the command of the God, those attendants of universal form, whose wealth was their asceticism, gratified Pārvatī with the specific manifestations of forms previously described. || 33 ||
The Great Goddess rejoices because of them, but Menā does not rejoice at all;
she indeed constantly feels disgust for both the god and the goddess. || 34 ||
But your husband Maheśvara, along with his retinue, is ill-behaved;
he is always poor, and his character is not at all fitting! || 35 ||
Mātrā, though addressed thus with words, could not endure it due to her feminine nature;
yet, having smiled, the bestower of boons then went to the side of Bhava. || 36 ||
With her face pale, the goddess addressed Mahādeva:
"I will not dwell here, O God; lead me to my own dwelling! || 37 ||
To do so, Mahādeva surveyed all the worlds for a place of residence;
O best of the twice-born, he chose the earth.
In Vārāṇasī, Mahādeva Maheśvara is the field of spiritual perfection.
Having learned that the city was occupied by Divodāsa, Bhava [departed]. (39)
Calling Nikumbha, who was standing at his side, he spoke these words:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, go to the city and make Vārāṇasī empty! (40)
That exceedingly powerful king [subdued him] by a mild means alone.
Then Nikumbha went to the city of Vārāṇasī.
In a dream, he showed himself to the barber named Maṅkaṇaka, saying:
"O sinless one, I shall bring you prosperity; prepare a place for me. || 42 ||
"Having fashioned an image in my likeness, install it at the edge of the city!
O brahmins, he then had everything done exactly as seen in the dream.
Having obtained the king's permission at the city gate according to the prescribed ritual, a great worship is indeed performed there constantly. || 44 ||
With perfumes, incenses, garlands, and likewise with sprinkled waters, as well as with various offerings of food and drink, it became, as it were, most wonderful. || 45 ||
In this manner, Gaṇeśvara is constantly worshipped there;
consequently, he bestows thousands of boons upon the Nāgas. || 46 ||
[She grants] sons, gold, long life, and likewise all desires.

But if the king should become angry with us, then the success of our undertaking would follow; from that, something [favorable] would proceed. Then, after a long time, anger took possession of the king. || 50 ||
"This being at the great gate of the Nāgas grants hundreds of boons when pleased; yet he gives us nothing at all! || 51 ||
"He is constantly worshipped by my people within my very city;
moreover, he has been entreated many times by my queen for the sake of a son. (52)
"And that ungrateful man, who eats his fill, does not even give me my son;

"Therefore, I shall destroy the abode of that evil-minded one.
Having thus resolved, that evil-minded sinner against the king [proceeded].
The evil-minded one destroyed that abode of Gaṇapati.
Seeing his sanctuary shattered, the Lord cursed the king: || 55 ||
"Since you have destroyed my dwelling place despite my innocence,
your city shall surely likewise become empty all at once! || 56 ||
Then, by that curse, Vārāṇasī became desolate;
having cursed the city, Nikumbha then approached Mahādeva. || 57 ||
And suddenly that city fled in every direction;
then, in that city, the Lord established his own abode,
for the Lord indeed delights there.
He took delight with the daughter of the mountain. || 58 ||
The god indeed finds no pleasure there due to the wonder of the house; "I dwell here, not in the city."
Then the goddess spoke to the god: || 59 ||
"I will not leave this dwelling, for my home is not yet liberated.
I will not go there;
go back to your own house, O Queen!"
The Blessed One, the three-eyed destroyer of Tripura, laughed and spoke.
Therefore, that very place was indeed declared by the Lord himself to be "Avimukta" (the Unreleased). Thus Vārāṇasī was cursed, and it is celebrated as Avimukta. || 61 ||
In that [place] dwells indeed the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose soul is established in Dharma, together with his Goddess, honored by all the gods throughout the three ages. || 62 ||
In the Kali age, that city of the Great-Souled One goes into concealment;
when that city has vanished, that [other] city dwells there once again. Thus was Vārāṇasī cursed, yet it returned once more to its habitation. || 63 ||
Formerly, the city of Vārāṇasī belonged to Bhadraśreṇya.
Bhadraśreṇya had a hundred sons who were preeminent archers. (64)
Having slain him, Divodāsa, the lord of men, established [himself there];
the kingdom of Bhadraśreṇya was seized by that more powerful one. || 65 ||
The son of Bhadraśreṇya was the renowned Durmada; because he was a child, he was released by Divodāsa out of compassion. || 66 ||
The lord of the earth indeed seized the inheritance of Haihaya;
by the high-souled Durmada, son of Bhadraśreṇya, he forcibly took back his paternal inheritance which had been seized by Divodāsa. || 66 ||
From Divodāsa, on the Dṛṣadvatī river, the hero Pratardana was born;
by that son, while still a boy, he indeed struck him back again.
O highly fortunate ones, by a Kṣatriya desiring to bring about the end of enmity, two sons of Pratardana, Vatsa and Bharga, became very famous. || 68 ||
Vatsaputra was indeed Alarka, and Saṃnati was his son.
Alarka, however, was the King of Kāśī, devoted to Brahmanas and true to his promise;
regarding that royal sage Alarka, an ancient verse has been sung by the ancients: || 69 ||
For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years,
that upholder of the Kāśi lineage remained young and endowed with beauty.
Through the grace of Lopāmudrā, he attained a supreme lifespan;
his kingdom was exceedingly great, and he himself was endowed with beauty and youth. || 71 ||
At the end of his curse, the mighty-armed king, having slain the Rākṣasa Kṣemaka, established the beautiful city of Vārāṇasī. || 72 ||
The heir of Saṃnati was the righteous one named Sunītha;
the heir of Sunītha, however, was the highly illustrious Kṣema.
Kṣema’s son was Ketumān; his son was Suketu; and the son of Suketu was known as Dharmaketu. || 74 ||
The heir of Dhārmaketu was the great chariot-warrior Satyaketu;
and the son of Satyaketu was the lord of subjects named Vibhu. || 75 ||
Suvibhu was the son of Vibhu, and Sukumāra was his son;
the son of Sukumāra, however, was the very righteous Dhṛṣṭaketu. || 76 ||
The heir of Dhṛṣṭaketu was Veṇuhotra, a lord of creatures;
and the son of Veṇuhotra was the lord of creatures named Bhārga. || 77 ||
Vatsa’s [son] was Vatsabhūmi, and Bhārgabhūmi was born from Bhārgava.
These were the sons of Aṅgiras, born in the lineage of Bhṛgu. || 78 ||
The three sons— Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas— were thousands in number.
These are declared to be the descendants of Kaśyapa through Raji.
Raji indeed begot five hundred sons here,
known as the Kṣatriyas called Rājeyas.
Then, when a most terrible war between the gods and the asuras had broken out, both the gods and the asuras spoke thus to the Grandfather: || 81 ||
"O Blessed One, who will be the victor in the battle between us two?
Tell us, O Lord of all beings, for we wish to hear it! (82)
Brahmā said:
"For whose sake the lord Raji, having taken up his weapons, shall fight in battle, they will conquer the three worlds; of this there is no doubt. || 83 ||
Where there is Rajas, there is fortitude, and there is prosperity; where there is fortitude,
there is both fortitude and prosperity.
In that case, righteousness as well as victory [shall prevail]. || 84 ||
Then those gods and Dānavas, delighted by what the god had said, approached Raji,
desiring victory.
They surrounded that bull among men. || 85 ||
For he was the son of Prabhā, the grandson of Svarbhānu,
a king of supreme splendor.
The increaser of the lunar dynasty. || 85 ||
All those gods and dānavas, with joyful minds, said to Rajī: "Take up this excellent bow for our victory! || 86 ||
Then Raji, who understood the matter, spoke there to those two— the god and the daitya— aiming at his own self-interest.
And manifesting his own glory: || 86 ||
"If, having conquered all the hosts of Daityas through my prowess, I become Indra by means of righteousness, then I shall fight in battle. (87)
The gods, with joyful minds, first responded:
"O King, may your desire be fulfilled exactly as you wish! (87)
Having heard the words of the hosts of gods, King Raji then questioned the leaders of the asuras just as he had questioned the gods. || 87 ||
The Dānavas, filled with pride, perceiving only their own self-interest, replied to that best of kings with these words full of arrogance: || 87 ||
Indra is our Prahlāda, for whose sake we are victorious;
at this time, however, you should remain as kings, impelled by the gods. || 88 ||
Saying "So be it," even as he was being urged by the gods, he was told by the gods, "O King, you shall become Indra after conquering [the demons]. (89)
He slew all the Dānavas who were otherwise invincible even to the wielder of the thunderbolt;
he, the self-controlled one of supreme glory, restored to the gods their lost prosperity.
Having slain all the Dānavas, the lord Raji took possession [of the kingdom].
Then Śatakratu, together with the gods, [confronted] the highly powerful Raji.
Having said, "I am the son of Raji," he spoke these words once more:
"O father, you are Indra among all the gods; of this there is no doubt. (92)
"I am your son, Indra, and I shall attain fame through my deeds.
But he, having heard Śakra’s words, was deceived by that [deity] through his illusory power.
"So be it," the king replied with joy to Śatakratu.
When that lord of the earth, who resembled a god, had thus ascended to heaven, [the people were struck with wonder]. 94.
From Indra, the sons of Raji obtained their inheritance according to custom;
those five hundred sons of his indeed occupied that station of the performer of a hundred sacrifices, the triple-heavened world of Svarga, in many places. || 95 ||
Then, after a long time had passed, the mighty Śakra, deprived of his kingdom and stripped of his sacrificial portion, spoke to Bṛhaspati: || 96 ||
"O Brahman-sage, prepare for me a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) the size of a jujube fruit, by which I may remain nourished with splendor. || 97 ||
"O Brahmin, I am emaciated, dejected, robbed of my kingdom, deprived of food, stripped of my vigor, weakened, and bewildered by the sons of Raji; be gracious to me! (98)
Bṛhaspati said:
O Śakra, if I had been urged by you in this manner even earlier, O sinless one, there would have been nothing that I would not have done for your sake. (99)

"I shall strive, O Lord of the Gods, for the sake of your welfare, O you of great splendor, so that you may regain your share and your kingdom before long. I will act accordingly, my dear; let your mind not be distressed! || 100 ||
Then he, the best among the wise, performed a great deed that increased his splendor and caused the delusion of intellect in them. || 101 ||
But when they became utterly deluded, intoxicated by passion, and unrighteous; when they became haters of Brahman and their vigor and prowess were destroyed, || 102 ||
Then Indra, having slain all the sons of Raji who were devoted to lust and anger, obtained sovereignty over the gods as well as that supreme station. || 103 ||
Whoever should hear or even retain this account of the displacement from his station and the restoration of Śatakratu shall never suffer from wickedness. || 104 ||
## Section 4. Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 3 | The Ṛṣis said:
How was the maiden given by the high-souled Marutta to the king?
And what was the power of those great-souled ones born from the daughter of the Maruts?
Sūta said:
Desiring food, that lord of creatures, the king of great splendor, used to consume the Marutsoma month after month for sixty years. || 12 ||
Pleased by that Marutsoma sacrifice, those Maruts, being delighted,
gave him inexhaustible food along with all desired articles of enjoyment.
His food, cooked but once, does not diminish for a day and night, even while being given away by the millions from the very time of sunrise. || 14 ||
From Mitrāyu and Kanyā, however, were born the sons of the wise Maruta;
from them were born beings of great essence, knowers of the Dharma, and perceivers of liberation. || 15 ||
Having renounced the duties of household life and attained dispassion, they reached the state of ascetics here and departed for union with Brahman. || 16 ||
Rambha was indeed childless; I shall now describe the lineage of Anenas: the son of Anenas was King...
The highly illustrious Pratikṣatra—1.
To Anenas was born the powerful Kṣatradharman;
to Kṣatradharman were born sons.
The Great Ascetic is the Antidote. || 1 ||
And the son of Pratikṣatra was the renowned Sañjaya;
Jaya was the son of Sañjaya, and Vijaya was his offspring. || 2 ||
The son of Vijaya was Kṛti; his son was Haryaśva; and the son of Haryaśva was the powerful King Sahadeva. || 3 ||
The righteous son of Sahadeva was known as Adīna;
Adīna’s son was Jayatsena, and Jayatsena’s son was Saṃkṛti. || 4 ||
The son of Saṃkṛti was also a righteous soul, a man of great fame who followed the dharma of a Kṣatriya.
These are declared to be the sinless ones; thus have these followers of the Kṣatriya dharma been described—learn now of Nahuṣa! Learn now of Nahuṣa! || 5 ||
The heirs of Nahuṣa were six of great prowess, possessing splendor equal to that of Indra; they were born of Virajā, the daughter of the Pitṛs.
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, Viyati, and Kṛti—of these, Yati was indeed the eldest, while Yayāti was the one born after him. || 7 ||
The most righteous one obtained the daughter of Kakutstha, named Gā, and the sage, having resorted to liberation, became one with Brahman. || 8 ||
Among those five, Yayāti was the lord of the earth; having conquered this world, he obtained Devayānī, the daughter of Uśanas, as his wife. (9)
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu, and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan and an Asura woman, likewise bore sons. || 10 ||
To him, Śakra, being pleased, gave a chariot of supreme brilliance, along with Druhyu, Anu, Pūru, and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
An unattached, divine golden chariot,
yoked with celestial, supreme horses that are bright and swift as thought.
By which one brings about the accomplishment of the task. || 12 ||
With that preeminent chariot,
the invincible Yayāti conquered the earth in six nights.
Likewise, [he conquered] the gods along with the Dānavas. || 13 ||
That chariot then became the property of all the Pauravas,
as long as the one named Vasu lived.
From Janamejaya, the Kaurava. || 14 ||
They begot sons of great prowess, resembling the sons of gods;
Śakra gave him a chariot.
Being pleased, [he beheld] that which was supremely radiant.
Unattached, divine, and golden,
along with two inexhaustible great quivers,
and yoked to horses as swift as thought.
By which he married a maiden. || 12 ||
Then Yayāti, invincible in battle, conquered the earth with that preeminent chariot.
By gods, dānavas, and humans. || 13 ||
He became the chariot for all the Paurava kings,
as long as they were born of noble lineage.
The Kauravas and Janamejayas. || 14 ||
The chariot of King Kuru’s son, the royal Pārikṣita, indeed went to its destruction through the curse of the wise Gārgya. || 15 ||
King Janamejaya indeed caused the violent death of Gārgya’s young son;
he thereby incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin. || 16 ||
That royal seer, smelling of iron, running hither and thither and abandoned by the people of the city and the countryside, found no peace at any time. || 17 ||
Then, tormented by grief, he found no peace anywhere;
in due course, he reached King Bārhadratha, the son of Bṛhadratha.
Then, having slain Jarāsaṃdha, Bhīma, the joy of the Kauravas, affectionately presented that excellent chariot to Vāsudeva. || 21 ||
Having reached old age and arrived at his own city,
Yayāti indeed spoke these words to his eldest and most excellent son, Yadu: || 22 ||
O father, old age has come upon me and gray hairs have spread over me;
yet, due to the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, I am not yet satiated with youth. (23)
O Yadu, accept this evil along with old age;
with your youth, I shall enjoy the objects of the senses. || 24 ||
When a full thousand years have passed,
I shall give you my youth and receive my own back.
May he cause my evil to decay along with old age. || 24 ||
Yadu said:
"O King, alms were promised by me to a Brāhmaṇa without being specifically designated; without having fulfilled that promise,"
I will not take on your old age. || 25 ||
But that [immortality] is indeed to be achieved through strenuous effort;
I will not accept your old age. || 25 ||
In old age, O King, there are many afflictions caused by the consumption of food and drink;
therefore, I am not able to accept old age from you. || 26 ||
Bearing white whiskers, dejected, and made infirm by old age, his body covered with wrinkles, he was unsightly and frail in appearance. || 27 ||
Incapable of performing his duties and humiliated in his youth,
along with his women— such old age I do not desire.
"O King, you have many sons who are dearer to you than I;
O knower of dharma, choose indeed another son to accept! || 29 ||
Thus addressed by Yadu, King Yayāti, the best among speakers, filled with anger, spoke while censuring his son: || 30 ||
"What other stage of life do you have, or what dharma is prescribed for you, O evil-minded one, that you disregard me, who am your instructor? (31)
Having spoken thus to Yadu, the king, filled with wrath, cursed him:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not yield your youth to me, O fool, your progeny shall have no kingdom; therefore, O fool, they shall not partake of sovereignty."
There is no doubt that you will become [a mother]; indeed, offspring shall be yours. || 32 ||
O best of the twice-born, the king spoke in this very same manner to Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu,
and he was likewise rejected by them.
The unconquered Yayāti, filled with extreme rage, cursed them.
(O best of the twice-born, this has been related by me exactly as it occurred previously. || 32 ||
Having thus cursed all four of his sons, beginning with Pūru, the king spoke those same words to Pūru as well, O twice-born ones. (32)
"O Pūru, if you so desire, I would roam this earth in my youth, having transferred my old age onto you, by means of your beauty. || 32 ||
The powerful Pūru accepted the old age of his father;
Yayāti, moreover, roamed the earth in the form of Pūru. || 32 ||
"O Turvasu, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age;
O dear son, I would indeed enjoy the objects of the senses through your youth. (33)
"When a full thousand years have passed, I shall give back your youth; I myself shall take back my own sin along with old age. (34)
Turvasu said:
"O father, I do not desire old age, which destroys the enjoyment of desires and brings an end to strength and beauty."
Which destroys both the intellect and the vital breath. || 35 ||
Yayāti said: "O Turvasu, since you, though born from my heart, do not grant me your youth, therefore your progeny shall come to total extinction. || 36 ||
O fool, you will become a king among those whose conduct is mixed with that of thieves, among those who act in a perverted manner, and among other flesh-eaters. || 37 ||

"You will undoubtedly be born among those who are attached to the wives of their gurus, among those who have entered the womb of animals, among those who follow the customs of cattle, and among the barbarians. || 38 ||
Having thus cursed his own son Turvasu, Yayāti spoke these words to Druhyu, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā: || 39 ||
"O Druhyu, do you undergo for a thousand years this old age that destroys complexion and form; in exchange, give me your own youth! || 40 ||
"When a full thousand years have passed, I shall restore your youth to you, and I myself shall take back my own wickedness along with old age. || 41 ||
Druhyu said:
"He eats neither elephant, nor chariot, nor horse; being aged, he enjoys no women.
He has no attachments, nor does he experience old age; for that reason, I do not desire him. || 42 ||
Yayāti said:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not grant me your youth, therefore, O Druhyu, your cherished desire shall never be fulfilled. || 43 ||

There, a constant movement of boats and crossing-places shall exist. You, along with your lineage, shall obtain the title "Arājabhoja" and the status of being of the Arājabhoja clan; you shall dwell there eternally. || 44 ||
Therefore, take upon yourself my evil along with old age;
for one thousand years, I shall live with your youth! || 45 ||
Anu said:
An old man eats like a child; an old man is as incapable as a child;
he eats food at the wrong time like one who is impure, for by old age he is always impure.
He does not offer oblations into the fires at the proper time; I do not desire such old age. || 46 ||
Yayāti said:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not grant me your youth, you shall therefore undergo this defect of old age that you have described. || 47 ||
Moreover, your subjects who have reached youth will perish;
and you yourself will likewise become intent on leaping into fire. || 48 ||
"O Pūru, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age;
for wrinkles, grey hair, and decrepitude have come over me, my son. (49)
"Due to the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, I am not yet satiated in my youth; therefore, for some time, I shall indeed enjoy the objects of the senses through your age. (50)
When a full thousand years have passed, I shall restore your youth, and I myself shall take back my own sin along with this old age. || 51 ||
Thus addressed, Pūru immediately replied to his father:
"O Great King, I shall do exactly as you have said; I will carry out your word."
But as you think, dear father, so shall I do. || 52 ||
"O King, I shall take upon myself your evil along with my old age;
take my youth from me and enjoy your desires as you wish. (53)
"Concealed by old age and assuming the form of one advanced in years, I shall give my youth to you and conduct myself according to my purpose. || 54 ||
Yayāti said: "O Pūru, I am pleased; may it be well with you. Being pleased, I grant this to you: your progeny shall be prosperous in their kingdom, having all their desires fulfilled. || 55 ||
Having spoken thus,
Yayāti, remembering Kāvya of the great vows, transferred his old age [to him].
Then, toward the high-souled Pūru. || 56 ||
But when the lord of men was still unsatiated with desires and enjoyments,
he then indeed [sought counsel] from the presence of his domestic priest.
He underwent his own old age. || 64 ||
Having attained those desires, the king, the lord of men, became both satisfied and weary; indeed, for a period of a thousand years, he reflected upon time. || 65 ||
Having calculated the divisions of time— the *kalās* and likewise the *kāṣṭhās*—
and perceiving that the time was complete, he spoke to his son Pūru.
"O subduer of enemies, O son, I have enjoyed the objects of the senses according to my pleasure, according to my energy, and according to the time, during my youth. (67)
"Pūra, I am pleased; may it be well with you. Take back your own youth and take this kingdom as well, for you are my son who has done what was dear to me. || 68 ||
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, underwent old age, while Pūru regained his own youth once again. || 69 ||
And when King Pūru desired to consecrate his youngest son, the social classes, headed by the Brahmins, spoke these words: || 70 ||
O Lord, how can you bypass Yadu, the grandson of Śukra and son of Devayānī, and grant the kingdom to Pūru, who is the youngest? || 71 ||
Your eldest son was Yadu; born after him was Turvasu; then the sons of Śarmiṣṭhā were Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru. || 72 ||
"How can the younger deserve the kingdom by bypassing the elder?
We inform you of this; uphold the Dharma! || 73 ||
Yayāti said:
"Let all the social orders, headed by the Brāhmaṇas, hear my words: that the kingdom must never, under any circumstances, be given by me to the eldest. (74)
A son who carries out the words of his parents is praised;
however, my eldest son Yadu has not obeyed my command. (75)
He who is contrary to his father is not considered a son by the virtuous;
he alone is a son who behaves toward his father and mother like a son. || 76 ||
I have been treated with contempt by Yadu, and likewise by Turvasu;
Druhyu and Anu as well have shown me extreme disregard. || 77 ||
The words spoken by Pūru were especially honored;
he is my youngest heir, by whom my old age was assumed. || 78 ||
"All my desires have been fulfilled by Pūru, who took the form of a son;
and Śukra himself, Kāvya Āśanas, granted me this boon. || 79 ||
O Lord of the Earth! Let that son who follows you, Puru, be consecrated in the kingdom with your approval as well. || 80 ||
The subjects (the people) said:
"A son who is endowed with virtues and is always devoted to the welfare of his parents deserves every auspicious thing; even if he is the youngest, he is the master. || 81 ||
"Pūru alone is worthy of this kingdom, he who is dear to you and does what is pleasing to you;
by virtue of Śukra’s boon, it is not possible to give a reply [to the contrary]. || 82 ||
Thus addressed by the contented citizens and country-folk,
the son of Nahuṣa (Purūravas) then consecrated his own son, Pūru, in his own kingdom.
He settled Turvasu in the southeastern direction,
and he appointed his eldest son, Yadu, in the northeastern direction.
In the midst of them, he consecrated Pūru as king; he was the son of Nahuṣa. || 84 ||
To Druhyu he gave the western region and to Anu the northern;
then King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, having conquered the earth with its seven islands and its oceans, divided it into five parts for his sons. || 85 ||
By them, this entire earth—with its seven continents and its cities—is protected according to their respective regions through righteousness by those who know the Dharma. || 86 ||
"O best of sages, I shall first describe their progeny.
Having set aside his bow and arrows, together with those five bulls among men..."
The king became old after having entrusted the burden to his kinsmen. || 87 ||
Having laid down his weapons and gazed upon the lords of the earth, King Yayāti, the unconquered, became filled with joy. || 87 ||
In this regard, these verses were sung of old by the great king Yayāti, by means of which one should withdraw desires from all sides, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs. (88)
Desires are never extinguished by the enjoyment of desires;
rather, like a fire fed with oblations, they increase all the more. || 89 ||
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist on earth—all that is not enough for even one person; having understood this, he is not deluded. || 90 ||
When one does not harbor an evil disposition toward any living being through action, mind, or speech, then one attains Brahman. || 91 ||
When one does not fear others, and when others do not fear him;
when one neither desires nor hates—then one attains Brahman. || 92 ||
That which is difficult for the foolish to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays, that disease which ends only with life—happiness belongs to him who renounces that craving. || 93 ||
The hair of an aging person decays; the teeth of an aging person decay;
but the hope for wealth and the hope for life do not decay even as one ages. || 94 ||

Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine happiness there may be, these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the exhaustion of craving. || 95 ||
For a full thousand years my mind was attached to sense objects;
nevertheless, craving for these arises in me day after day. (951)
Therefore, having abandoned her, I shall direct my mind toward Brahman; becoming free from the pairs of opposites and free from the sense of "mine," I will wander with the deer.
Having spoken thus, that royal sage entered the forest together with his wife;
and after a long time,
he practiced extensive austerities.
Having performed austerities on Bhṛgutuṅga,
at the conclusion of his penance, the highly illustrious one cast off his body by fasting.
Together with his wife, he attained heaven. || 97 ||
In his lineage, O best of sages,
there were five most excellent royal seers by whom the entire earth was pervaded, just as by the rays of the sun. || 98 ||
O best of the twice-born, by reading or hearing this meritorious account of Yayāti’s life, a man shall become blessed, possessed of offspring, long-lived, and renowned. || 99 ||
## Section 4: The Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 4 While residing in Dvāravatī, Prasena obtained from the Sun a great, divine jewel named Syamantaka. (1)
The Sun became a friend to that Satrājit, equal to his very life. Once, at the end of the night, that best of chariot-warriors set out on his chariot.
He went to the water to touch it and to worship the sun;
as he was standing there worshipping the sun, Vivasvat stood before him.
Then the Lord Vivasvat, whose form was indistinct and who possessed a circle of radiance, being all-pervading, spoke to the King who stood before him: || 3 ||
Just as I always behold you in the sky, O Lord of lights, the god encircled by a halo of splendor, even so do I see you standing before me. || 4 ||
"What distinction is there for me, who has approached you as a friend?
Having heard this, the Blessed One [offered] the Syamantaka jewel.
Then the Lord, having unfastened it from his own neck, placed it aside;
thereupon the king then beheld it in embodied form. || 6 ||
Then, having seen him, Satrajit was filled with joy and conversed with him for a moment;
as Vivasvat was about to depart, Satrajit addressed him once more.
"You illuminate these worlds; O Lord, you whom Agnisavarna proclaimed as such, by whom the world constantly beholds [you]—O Blessed One, you ought to grant me this very jewel-gem! || 8 ||
Then the Sun-god gave him the Syamantaka jewel;
having fastened it on, the lord of the earth entered the city. || 9 ||
The people ran after him, crying out, "Ah! This is Sūrya who is going! But the king was filled with wonder at his own city as well as his inner apartments. || 10 ||
King Satrājit, out of affection, gave that divine and supreme jewel-gem Syamantaka to his brother Prasenajit. || 11 ||

That jewel, known as Syamantaka, which was in the dwelling of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, yielded gold; in whatever kingdom it remained, the rain-god poured forth rain in due season, and there was indeed no fear of disease. || 12 ||
Prasena, however, desired the Syamantaka jewel;
Govinda did not obtain it, and although he was capable of doing so, he did not seize it. || 13 ||
Once, while out on a hunt adorned with that [jewel], Prasena met his death at the hands of a forest-dwelling lion because of the Syamantaka. || 14 ||
Then the mighty king of bears, having struck down the charging lion, took that precious jewel.
Having taken it, he entered a hole. || 15 ||
Then the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, having learned of that request for the jewel on account of the killing of Prasenajit, [approached] Kṛṣṇa.
Everyone indeed suspected this. || 16 ||
Suspected [of the crime], that righteous-souled one,
having not performed that deed,
said: "I shall bring back the jewel."
Having made this promise, he went to the forest. || 17 ||
Then, having taken up the tracks of Prasena with trustworthy men, they followed them to the place where Prasena had been hunting.
Searching for the excellent mountain Ṛkṣavanta and the supreme mountain Vindhya, the high-minded one, exhausted, beheld them.
He found Prasena killed along with his horse, but he did not find that jewel;
then, the lion was nearby the body of Prasena. (20)
He saw that he had been killed by a bear; the bear, however, was indicated by its footprints.
Following those tracks, Mādhava then reached the cave of the bear. || 21 ||

O twice-born ones, in a large cave, he heard a voice uttered by a woman intoxicated with joy; she was the nurse who, having taken the prince—the son of Jāmbavat—was saying, "Do not cry," while playing with a jewel. || 22 ||
Jāmbavān, the king of the bears,
indeed slew that lion and took away the divine jewel.
He entered his own cave. || 15 ||
Then the elders of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas considered that deed of Kṛṣṇa to have been committed out of greed for the jewel.
They suspected him alone. || 16 ||
The powerful Lord, the slayer of enemies, could not tolerate that false accusation against them.
He wandered through the forest. || 17 ||
"The lion killed Prasena; the lion was slain by Jāmbavān. Do not weep, my dear child; for this Syamantaka belongs to you! || 23 ||
Having made himself known, that sound quickly entered the cave;
and near the mouth of the cave, he saw Prasena torn apart.
Then the Blessed One entered that bear’s cave directly. (24)
Having stationed the Yadus at the entrance of the cave along with Balarāma,
the wielder of the Śārṅga bow remained by the one staying within the cave.
He beheld Jāmbavanta. || 25 ||
The noble-minded one beheld Jāmbavān, the king of the bears. || 25 ||
Vāsudeva, however, fought with Jāmbavān inside the cave; Govinda fought with his bare arms alone for twenty-one days.
But when Kṛṣṇa had entered the cave, those led by Vasudeva returned to Dvāravatī and announced that Kṛṣṇa was slain. || 27 ||
Having conquered the mighty Jāmbavān, Vāsudeva obtained the maiden Jāmbavatī, who was highly esteemed by the king of the bears. || 28 ||
Overwhelmed by the Lord’s splendor, Jāmbavān quickly gave the jewel and his daughter Jāmbavatī to Viṣvaksena. || 28 ||
He took the Syamantaka jewel for the sake of his own purification,
and having instructed the king of the bears, he then emerged from the cave.
By means of a stratagem, Kṛṣṇa departed for Dvārakā without those who had been his precursors.
Having thus recovered the jewel and cleared his own name, Acyuta presented it to Satrājit in the assembly of all the Sāttvatas.
Thus, though falsely accused,
Kṛṣṇa purified himself from the sin of killing his enemy.
Having completely conquered the Syamantaka [jewel]. || 31 ||
He who knows how this false accusation against Kṛṣṇa was dispelled here shall never again be touched by a false accusation. || 31 ||
Satrājit had ten wives, and from them there were a hundred sons;
among them, three were famous, the eldest being Bhaṅgakāra.
Vīra, Vātapati, and likewise Upasvāvan—
these always sought after the blameless Satyabhāmā, while Akrūra sought an opportunity to seize both her and the Syamantaka jewel. || 36 ||
Then, having slain Satrājit at night, the mighty Śatadhanvan took that jewel and gave it to Akrūra. || 37 ||
Then Akrūra, that bull among men, taking that jewel, made an agreement: "I am not to be informed by you. || 38 ||
We shall come to your aid when you are assailed by Kṛṣṇa;
today, without a doubt, the entire city of Dvārakā stands under my control. || 39 ||
When her father was dead, the high-minded Satyabhāmā, afflicted with grief, ascended a chariot and departed for the city of Vāraṇāvata. || 40 ||
But Satyabhāmā, having reported that conduct of Śatadhanvan, the Bhoja king, to her husband, was afflicted with grief and shed tears from her eyes as she stood by his side. || 41 ||
After performing the water-libation rites for the deceased Pāṇḍavas, Hari then appointed Sātyaki to the task of providing funeral offerings for them.
Then, having arrived swiftly at Dvārakā, the illustrious Madhusūdana spoke these words to his elder brother, the wielder of the plow: || 43 ||
Prasena was killed by a lion, and Satrājit by Śatadhanvan; but the Syamantaka jewel shall come to me, for I am its master, O Lord. (44)
Therefore, mount the chariot quickly; having slain the great car-warrior Bhoja, O mighty-armed one, that Syamantaka jewel shall belong to us! || 45 ||
Then a tumultuous battle commenced between the Bhoja king and Kṛṣṇa;
thereafter, Śatadhanvan looked in every direction for Akrūra. || 46 ||
Seeing both Bhoja and Janārdana enraged there,
Akrūra, though capable, did not pursue the son of Hṛdika out of deceit.
Then, afflicted by fear, the Bhoja king set his mind on retreat;
he retreated from his heart a full hundred yojanas. || 48 ||
The divine mare of Bhoja, renowned by the name Hṛdayā and capable of traveling a hundred yojanas, was the one with which he fought against Kṛṣṇa. || 49 ||
Seeing that his horses were exhausted from the hundred-yojana journey and observing the superior speed of his own chariot, he struck Śatadhanvan.
Then, O twice-born ones, due to the exhaustion and fatigue of that mare, her life-breaths ascended into the sky; thereupon Kṛṣṇa spoke to Rāma: || 51 ||
"Stay here, O mighty-armed one; the faults of horses have been seen by me.
I shall go on foot and seize the Syamantaka jewel. || 52 ||
Then, having gone on foot from there, Acyuta, the supreme knower of weapons, struck Śatadhanvan near Mithilā.
Having slain the mighty Bhoja, he did not see the Syamantaka;
and as Kṛṣṇa was returning, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) said to him, "Give me the jewel. || 54 ||
Kṛṣṇa said, "It does not exist," whereupon Rāma, filled with rage, repeatedly replied to Janārdana with the exclamation, "Fie! || 55 ||
Because we are brothers, I forgive this; may it be well with you, I am departing.
I have no concern for Dvārakā, nor for you, nor for the Vṛṣṇis! || 56 ||
Then Rāma, the crusher of enemies, entered Mithilā, honored by the King of Mithilā with all desired offerings. || 57 ||
At that very time, however, Babhru, the best among the wise, performed all kinds of sacrifices without restraint. || 58 ||
For the sake of the Syamantaka jewel, the wise and highly illustrious son of Gāndinī entered this initiation along with his armor for the purpose of protection. || 59 ||
Then, for sixty years, that righteous-souled king employed other jewels and various kinds of wealth solely for the performance of sacrifices. || 60 ||
Those sacrifices of that great-souled one were known as the Akrūra-yajñas;
they all provided abundant food and sacrificial fees, and granted every desire. || 61 ||
Then King Duryodhana, that lord, having gone to Mithilā,
obtained from Balabhadra the divine instruction in the use of the mace.
Then Rāma was propitiated by the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans, and he was brought back to Dvārakā itself by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa. || 63 ||

But Akrūra, that bull among men and possessor of great strength, having slain Satrājit in battle along with his kinsmen, departed together with the Andhakas after having killed Śatrughna and his followers in the fight. || 64 ||
To the two sons of Narā,
the daughter of Svaphalka, were born two renowned and exceedingly powerful sons, Bhaṅgakāra and Ya.
Two sons were born to the chief of the Andhakas, Śatrughna and Bandhumat;
yet Kṛṣṇa was not pleased with the slaying of Bhaṅgakāra.
Out of fear of causing a rift among his kinsmen, Kṛṣṇa likewise overlooked that matter. When Akrūra had thus departed, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain. || 65 ||
Then, due to a drought, the kingdom became exceedingly weakened in many ways;
consequently, the Kukuras and Andhakas propitiated Akrūra. || 66 ||
Then, when that lord of donors had arrived again at Dvāravatī,
the thousand-eyed Indra rained down upon the shore of the ocean.
And for the sake of pleasing Vāsudeva, the illustrious Akrūra, that bull among the Yadus, gave his own sister, a maiden esteemed for her virtuous character. || 68 ||
Then, having discerned through his yoga that the jewel had gone to Akrūra, Janārdana Kṛṣṇa spoke to Akrūra while he was in the midst of the assembly hall: || 69 ||
O Lord, worthy of honor, grant me that jewel, that excellent gem which has come into your hands; do not show me disrespect by withholding it! || 70 ||
When sixty years had passed, the anger that arose within me grew repeatedly; thus, a great lapse of time occurred. || 71 ||
Then, at the word of Kṛṣṇa, the high-minded Babhru, in the assembly of all the Sātvatas, gave that jewel away without any difficulty. || 72 ||
Then Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of enemies, with a joyful heart, gave that jewel back to Babhru from Babhru’s hand, as it had been obtained through Babhru's honesty. || 73 ||
Having received the Syamantaka jewel from Kṛṣṇa’s hand and fastened it on, the son of Gāndinī shone like the sun. || 74 ||
He who knows this false accusation, this false accusation uttered against Kṛṣṇa, and also his supreme purity—
false accusations do not affect him.
They never touch it at any time. || 75 ||
O Veda, he shall never incur a false accusation in any way whatsoever. || 75 ||
From Anamitra was born Chini, the youngest son of Vṛṣṇi; from him came Śaineya Satyaka, and from him Yuyudhāna Sātyaki. || 1 ||
Two sons were born to Mādrī, namely the renowned Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka;
likewise, two sons, Śvaphalka and Citraka, were born to Vṛṣṇi. || 2 ||
Satyavāk was endowed with truth, and Satyaka was his son. || 1 ||
Sātyaki was Yuyudhāna, and his son was Bhūti;
Bhūti’s son was Yugandhara.
Thus has the Bhautya [manvantara] been proclaimed. || 1 ||
To Mādrī’s son Yudhājit, however, was born a son, Vṛṣṇi,
as well as Citraka. || 2 ||
Wherever the great king Śvaphalka, whose soul is righteous, resides, there is no fear of disease, nor likewise any fear of drought. || 3 ||
Once, O best of the twice-born, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain for three years within the realm of the powerful King of Kāśī.

There he caused Śvaphalka, who was highly honored, to dwell; and through Śvaphalka’s presence there, Indra, whose vehicle is green horses, sent down rain— Indra, the subduer of Pāka, poured forth rain.
Śvaphalka took as his wife the daughter of the King of Kāśī, named Gāndinī, for she used to give a cow daily to a brāhmaṇa. || 6 ||
Indeed, while staying within her mother’s womb for many groups of years, she did not give birth; and as she remained thus in the womb, her father spoke to her: || 7 ||
"Be born quickly; may it be well with you; for what reason do you remain?
Thus spoke that maiden from within the womb to him day after day.
"If you would grant it, then, O father, may I emerge from the womb once my desire is fulfilled.
Having said "So be it," her father fulfilled her wish. || 9 ||

From him was born Akrūra, a donor, a sacrificer, a hero, learned, and fond of guests; his son, known as Akrūra, was the son of Śvaphalka and was liberal in giving sacrificial fees. || 10 || Śvāphalka was Bhūridakṣiṇa. || 10 ||
Upamadgu, Madgu, Mudara, Arimejaya, Girirakṣas, Upekṣa, Śatrughna, and Arimardana. || 11 ||
Dharmabhṛt, Yatidharma, Gṛdhramojas, Antaka, as well as Āvāha, Prativāha, and the beautiful woman Sundarī. || 12 ||
She was the queen of Viśrutāśva, and her daughter was Vasuṃdharā;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, and was enchanting to all living beings.
From Akrūra and Ugrasenī were born two sons who brought joy to their lineage, Devavān and Upadeva, both resembling gods. || 13 ||
Citraka had sons: Pṛthu, Vipṛthu, Aśvagrīva, Aśvabāhu, Supārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa. (14)
Ariṣṭanemi, Aśva, Sudharmā, Dharmabhṛt, Subahu, and Bahubahu; Śraviṣṭhā and Śravaṇā were the two women. || 15 ||
From Andhaka, the daughter of Kaśya obtained four sons:
Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śami, and Kambalabarhiṣa. || 16 ||
Kukura’s son was Vṛṣṇi, and Vṛṣṇi’s son was Kapotaroman; his son, in turn, was Tittiri. || 17 ||
He had a learned son named Nala, who was a friend of Tumburu; it is said that the drum which resounded with the scent of sandalwood water is known by his name. || 17 ||

From him Punarvasu was born, and from him also Abhijit was born as a son; thus Abhijit was born from Punarvasu. Once born, however, Punarvasu—the best of men—performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son. || 18 ||
In the midst of that *atirātra* sacrifice, he arose from the center of the *sadas*;
he was wise, a knower of dharma, a donor, a performer of sacrifices, and possessed of abundant wealth. || 18 ||
In this way, it is said that a pair of children was born to Abhijit:
Āhuka and Āhukī, both renowned as the best among those who possess fame. || 19 ||
And regarding this, they cite these verses concerning that Āhuka:
"He [fought] against those [forces] equipped with quivers, yoked to chariots, with their axle-trees, banners, and protective fenders. (20)
There were indeed ten thousand chariots with a roar like thunderclouds;
there was no one among them who was without a son, none who had not given a hundred gifts, and none who did not possess a hundred thousand weapons.
Neither of impure conduct nor one who has not sacrificed,
he who would go to the feast from afar—
great as a young colt, surrounded by a white retinue. || 22 ||
Accompanied by eighty chariots, Āhuka went first;
it is said that they set out toward the eastern direction for the sake of the Nāgas of Bhoja.
There are twenty-one thousand girdles of silver and gold;
there are just as many thousands in that northern direction as well. || 24 ||
It is said that the Kiṅkiṇī remained with the Bhojas, the protectors of the earth,
and Āhukī also [remained] with the people of Avanti.
The Andhakas gave their sister [in marriage]. || 25 ||
To Āhuka, however, two sons were born of Kāśyā:
Devaka and Ugrasena, both of whom were equal to the offspring of gods. || 26 ||
Devaka had four sons who were like the gods:
Devavān, Upadeva, Sudeva, and [Deva].
There were seven maidens; he gave them to Vasudeva:
Devakī and Śāntidevā, and the others.
Sudevā is protected by the gods. || 28 ||
Vṛkadevī, Upadevī, and Sunāmnī was the seventh; and Āhuka [ruled] among the Avantīs.
But he gave his own sister Āhukī [to Akrūra]. || 25 ||
From Āhuka, two sons were born to the daughter of Kāśya:
the heroic sons of Devaka.
Devarakṣita was born, resembling a god among the thirty. || 27 ||
They had seven sisters,
whom he gave to Vasudeva:
Vṛkadevā and Upadevā, and...
Likewise, there was another, Devarakṣitā. || 28 ||
Śrīdevā, Śāntidevā, Sahadevā, and another; Devakī was the seventh among them.
Sunāmā and Carudarśanā;
these were the nine sons of Ugrasena, and among them, Kaṃsa was the eldest. || 29 ||
Nyagrodha, Sunāman, Kaṅka, Śaṅku, Subhūṣaṇa, Rāṣṭrapāla, and Sutanu; [and] Sutanū, Rāṣṭrapāla, Anādhrṣṭi, and Puṣṭimān; [and] Yuddhamuṣṭi and Supuṣṭimān. || 30 ||
They had fifty sisters: Kaṃsā, Kaṃsavatī, Sutanū, Rāṣṭrapālī, and the beautiful woman Kaṅkā. || 31 ||
Ugrasena, along with his offspring, has been described as born of the Kukura line.
By upholding this lineage of the Kukurans, who possess immeasurable splendor, a man shall become possessed of progeny and attain an extensive lineage for himself. || 32 ||
The son of Bhajamāna was Vidūratha, the foremost of chariot-warriors;
and Rājadhideva, the heroic son of Vidūratha, came after him. || 33 ||
The daughter of Rājadhideva was born to that Śūra, and from him were born sons of even greater heroism; they were born exceedingly powerful:
Datta and Atidatta, both mighty, as well as Vāta and Nivāta.
He whose horses are crimson and whose vehicle is drawn by white steeds. || 34 || He whose horses are crimson and whose vehicle is drawn by white steeds. || 34 ||
Śamī and Dattaśarman; Śamī and Gadavarman, and Dantaśatru, the conqueror of enemies; indeed, Nidānta was the conqueror of enemies. || 35 ||
Śravaṇā and Śraviṣṭhā were born as sisters. || 35 ||
Śamīputra was Pratikṣatra; the son of Pratikṣatra was Svayaṃbhoja, and from Svayaṃbhoja, Hṛdika was born. || 36 ||
He indeed had sons; the sons of Hṛdika were all of terrible prowess—ten of them of terrible prowess—with Kṛtavarman as the eldest among them, and Śatadhanvan as the middle one. || 37 ||
Devānta and Narānta, Devārha and Subāhu,
the physician Vaitaraṇa and the physician Vaitaraṇa,
Sudānta and Atidānta, and Sudānta and Adhidānta.
Nikāśya is the deceiver of desire. Kanaka is born from gold.
Devānta had a son named Devārha; the learned Devārha was the son of Kambalabarhiṣ. From Kambalabarhiṣ was born Asamaujas, and he had two sons, both of whom were named Asamaujas. || 39 ||
To Asamaujas, who was childless, he gave his sons Sudarśana, Sucāru, and Kṛṣṇa; these are known as the Andhakas. || 40 ||
Whoever should constantly recite this lineage of the Andhakas obtains for himself a vast lineage; of this there is no doubt. (401)
He begot the heroic Devamīḍhuṣa upon Aśmakī;
and ten sons were born to Śūra from his queen Bhojā. || 41 ||
The mighty-armed Vasudeva was born first as Ānakadundubhi, at whose birth the kettledrums resounded in heaven. || 42 ||
A very great clamor of kettledrums arose in the sky, and a great rain of flowers fell upon the hero’s palace. (43)
Even throughout the entire world of men, there was no one on earth equal in beauty to that foremost of men; his splendor was like that of the moon. || 44 ||
From him Devabhāga was born, and from him again Devaśravas;
then Anādhṛṣṭi, Kanavaka, Anādhṛṣṭivṛka, Vatsavān, Gṛñjama, Nandana, and Śṛñjaya. || 45 ||
Śyāma, Śamīka, and Gaṇḍūṣa were his [sons], and he had five excellent daughters:
Pṛthukīrti, Pṛthā, Śrutadevā, Śrutaśravā, and Śrutakīrti. (46) Śrutadevā and Śrutaśravā. (46)
Rājādhidevī was likewise one of these five mothers of heroes.
Kunti made Pṛthā her daughter, and Pāṇḍu married her. || 47 ||
The heroic [Pṛthu] gave her to Kuntibhoja, who was venerable and aged;
therefore, Pṛthā, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, became renowned as Kuntī. || 48 ||
From him, the hero of the Kurus and chief of the Pāṇḍus, Pṛthā obtained a wife;
from her, she gave birth to three sons whose splendor was equal to fire—heroes who were unrivaled chariot-warriors in the world and possessed prowess equal to Śakra. || 48 ||
In her was born that king who knew the dharma; from Dharma, the knower of dharma begot his son Yudhiṣṭhira, and from Māruta he begot Vṛkodara,
Bhīmasena, likewise from the Wind.
And from Indra himself came Dhanañjaya,
the hero who is without rival in the world,
whose prowess is equal to that of Śakra. || 49 ||
To Pṛthukīrti was born a son of Vṛddhaśarman,
the heroic and mighty Dantavakra, the lord of Karūṣa. || 50 ||
To Kaikeyī Śrutakīrti was born the mighty Saṃtardana;
likewise Cekitāna and Bṛhatkṣatra, both of great strength;
and Vinda and Anuvinda, the two brothers from Avanti, who were exceedingly powerful. (50)
And from Śrutaśravā was born Śiśupāla, the king of the Cedis,
who was formerly the Daitya king Hiraṇyakaśipu. || 51 ||
The son of the royal sage Damaghoṣa was one of renowned prowess, who in a former life became that ten-necked crusher of enemies;
likewise, Kumbhakarṇa was his younger brother, as well as the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa. || 51 ||
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the heroic sons of Vasudeva;
indeed, by upholding this threefold, highly energetic, and extensively branched lineage of Vṛṣṇi, one is not joined with misfortunes in this world. || 51 ||
The fourteen excellent women who were the wives of Vasudeva—
these were indeed the wives of Vasudeva.
There were thirteen excellent women:
Pauravī named Rohiṇī, and another, Madirā;
likewise Vaiśākhī, Bhadrā, and Sunāmnī as the fifth. (52)
Sahadevā, Śāntidevā, Śrīdevā, Devarakṣitā, Vṛkadevā, Upadevā, and Devakī as the seventh;
Sutanu and Vaḍavā likewise.
These two are attendants. || 53 ||
Pauravī, named Rohiṇī, was the daughter of Bāhlīka;
she was the eldest and most illustrious wife, beloved by Anakadundubhi. || 54 ||
He obtained as his sons the eldest, Rāma, as well as Sāraṇa, Śaṭha, Durdama, Damana, Śubhra, Piṇḍāraka, and Uśīnara. || 55 ||
And [he begot] a daughter named Citrā, while nine [others] were born from Rohiṇī. From Vasudeva and Devakī was born the highly illustrious Śauri.
And from Rāma, Niśaṭha was born as a beloved son by Revatī. || 56 ||
Pārśvī and Pārśvamardī, Śiśu and Satyadhṛti, Mandabāhya, Rāmāṇaka, Girika, and Girin. || 561 ||
Śulkagulma, Atigulma, and Daridrāntaka;
and there are also five other maidens—learn their names:
Arciṣmatī, Sunandā, Surasā, and likewise Suvacā.
Likewise Śatabalā; these were the daughters of Sāraṇa: || 563 ||
Bhadrāśva, Bhadragupti, and likewise Bhadraviṣṭa; Bhadrabāhu, Bhadraratha, and likewise Bhadrakalpa. || 564 ||
Supārśvaka, Kīrtimān, and Rohitāśva were the sons of Śaṭha.
Durdama, Abhibhūta, Nanda, Upananda, Mitra, Kukṣimitra, and Bala are known as those born in the lineage of Rohiṇī. || 56 ||
Citrā, Upacitrā, Kṛtakā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and then Apsarā—these daughters of Madirā were indeed born from Vasudeva. || 56 ||
Upabimba and Bimba, as well as Sattvavanta and Mahaujas—these four are renowned as the sons of Bhadra, possessed of great strength. || 56 ||
Vaiśākhyā gave birth to Śauri’s excellent son Kauśika; from Śauri, Suṣeṇa and Kīrtimān were also born of Devakī.
Udāyī, Bhadrasena, and Rjudāya as the fifth, and Bhadravideha as the sixth—Kaṃsa slew them all. || 56 ||
Then, in that state, the Lord of the World became manifest once more as the venerable Viṣṇu, who was formerly Kṛṣṇa, the Prajāpati.
Subhadrā, the sweet-spoken lady, was born as one who followed after Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇā was further explained as Subhadrā, the delight of the Vṛṣṇis;
from Pārtha, through Subhadrā, the chariot-warrior Abhimanyu was born. || 57 ||
[From Akrūra, Satyaketu was born of the daughter of Kāśī. Now, learn by name those heroic sons who were born to Vasudeva from his seven highly fortunate wives: || 58 ||
From Pūrvadyu and Sahadevā were born sons who were indeed heroic;
from Śūra was born Śāntideva, the upholder of the lineage, who begot Janastamba. || 58 ||
Upasanga and Vasu were his two sons protected by the gods;
thus he had ten sons, and Kaṃsa put them all to death. || 58 ||
Both Bhoja and Vijaya were the sons of Śāntidevā;
Vṛkadeva was born of Sudevā.
And Gada—these two were his sons. || 59 ||
Vṛkadevī, the daughter of the king of the Vigartas and the wife of Śīśirāyaṇa, gave birth to the high-souled Agāva. || 60 ||
Devakī gave birth to a son named Sura, O noble one, who was a seeker of truth, highly fortunate, and a versatile warrior in battle. || 60 ||
O twice-born ones, while wandering in the city garden (or forest) of Śrāddhadevī,
Śauri begot an imperishable son, Kauśika, upon a Vaiśya woman.
Sugandhī and Vanarājī were the two wives of Śauri.
Puṇḍra and Kapila were the two sons of Sugandhī;
of these two, Puṇḍra became king, while Kapila went to the forest. || 60 ||
In another [womb], the heroic and powerful son of Vasudeva was born;
he was that Niṣāda named Jarā, the foremost of archers. || 60 ||
Uddhava was the highly fortunate son of Devabhāga;
they declare Devaśravas to be the most excellent among the learned. || 65 ||
From Aśmakī, Anādṛṣṭi obtained a glorious son,
Nivṛttaśatru Śatrughna, who was a god of the ancestral rites and possessed great strength.
From him was born Śrāddhadeva, who is renowned as the son of Niṣadha;
he was the exceedingly heroic Ekalavya, brought up among the Niṣādas. || 67 ||
To Gaṇḍūṣa, who was childless,
Viṣvaksena gave two sons:
Cārudeṣṇa and Śudeṣṇa.
The Pañcāla [region] is characterized by auspicious marks. || 68 ||
O best of the twice-born, that mighty-armed son of Rukmiṇī, the younger brother, was never one to turn back from battle, O heroes. || 68 ||
Thousands of crows followed behind him as he went, thinking, "Today we shall feast upon the beautiful bodies of those slain by Cārudeṣṇa. || 68 ||
Tantrīja and Tantrīpāla were the two sons of Kanavaka;
and to Vṛka, who was indeed childless, the powerful Vasudeva [gave them]. (69)
Śauri gave his son Saumitri, and Kauśika likewise gave his son Vīra; then there were the two heroic sons of Gr̥ñjima, Vīru and Aśvahanu. || 70 ||
Śyāmaputra was Śamīka; Śamīka, however, governed the kingdom while loathing the state of being a Bhoja.
He performed the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 71 ||
Ajātaśatru was born as the destroyer of his enemies. || 71 ||
Disgusted with the state of being a mere enjoyer,
he attained the status of a royal sage; he undertook an inquiry into human effort, yet he did not transcend that very effort.
Likewise, in the twelfth year, he has the appearance of black iron. || 711 ||
But Gārgya, falsely accused and impelled by wrath, took a cowherd’s daughter and proceeded to engage in sexual intercourse with her. || 712 ||
The Apsaras Gopālī, assuming the guise of a cowherd woman,
bore for Gārgya the embryo that was difficult to sustain, Acyuta.
By the command of Śūlapāṇi, he was born as a king of great strength named Kālayavana from Mānuṣī, the wife of Gārgya. || 704 ||
Horses with the forebodies of bulls carried him in battle;
meanwhile, that infant grew up in the inner apartments of the childless king.
O best of sages, that son of Yavana became Kālayavana.
Desiring battle, that king questioned the most excellent of the twice-born;
the powerful Nārada then told him about the clan of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
Then, with an army consisting of an akṣauhiṇī, he marched toward Mathurā. || 707 ||
He dispatched a messenger to the abode of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas;
then the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, placing the high-minded Kṛṣṇa at their head, [set out].
Having assembled, they then consulted one another out of fear of Yavana;
having reached a decision, they all resolved upon flight. || 709 ||
Leaving the beautiful city of Mathurā while honoring the wielder of the Pināka bow, they desired to establish their residence in Kuśasthalī, Dvāravatī.
Thus, a wise man who is pure and has his senses restrained should recite this birth-story of Kṛṣṇa on the sacred festival days.
Free from debt, he shall become happy. || 72 ||
Whoever, firm in their vows, should read this account of Kṛṣṇa’s birth, or even cause a Brāhmaṇa to hear it;
One shall attain very great happiness. || 72 ||
